## First Preface.

### To the lovers of truth, grace and light through Jesus Christ!

§. 1.

There is a great and almost universal complaint which has arisen in recent days within the church that calls itself "orthodox," and which continues to this day, concerning the perverted zeal of those reform-hungry newcomers <note>The original German "Reformations-süchtig" implies an unhealthy or obsessive craving for change.</note> and critics. These individuals emerged some years ago with a most harmful poison, rejecting, among many other wholesome things, the <term>systematic method <note>original: "methodum systematicam"</note></term> in theology. At the same time, they discard those textbooks that utilize such a method—the <term>systems <note>original: "systemata"</note></term> and <term>summaries of theology <note>original: "summas Theologiæ"</note></term>—turning up their noses at the academic style of teaching and systematic order, as one might put it. Yet, this method of teaching is intended to be nothing other than a thorough and detailed presentation of Christian doctrine in a good order. According to its own description, it is a genre of books in which this doctrine is presented in a well-arranged manner, with an orderly division and connection of what is otherwise found scattered here and there in the <term>Holy Scripture</term>. Furthermore, it serves to indicate both erroneous teachings (and what might give occasion for error) and their refutation, for the easier and better comprehension and understanding of the articles of faith and mysteries—or the <term>faith which is believed <note>original: "fidei, quæ creditur"</note></term> and <term>orthodoxy <note>correct belief</note></term>. This is provided as an aid to the intellect and memory, especially for those who intend to teach others, acting as a portrait and model of the correct <term>analogy of faith <note>original: "analogiæ fidei," translated by the author as "Glaubens-Aehnlichkeit" or the internal consistency of biblical truths.</note></term>.

§. 2. What just and fair cause one has for such complaints can best be recognized by anyone who knows what store of provisions can be found in these storehouses during a time of scarcity, when a...

<summary>This preface defends the use of systematic theology and structured textbooks against contemporary critics who viewed such academic methods as unnecessary or harmful to the faith. The author argues that these "systems" are essential tools for organizing biblical truth and training future teachers.</summary>
<keywords>systematic theology, orthodoxy, church reform, pedagogy, Holy Scripture, analogy of faith, religious polemics</keywords>

## First Preface.

...hunger comes into the land according to the word of the Lord; and yet all the bookshelves, <term>museums <note>In this period, a "museum" referred to a study, library, or place dedicated to the muses and learning.</note></term>, lecterns, schools, and churches are as full of <term>systems <note>original: "systemata"</note></term>, <term>compendiums <note>original: "Compendia"</note></term>, and God’s alone soul-saving Word as there is sand by the sea and as the heavens are full of stars. For what does it matter if the natural man <note>The "natural man" refers to someone who is unregenerate or living by human reason alone, without spiritual enlightenment.</note> can rejoice a little in this light and strut about with it, when it must eventually become quite dark and be extinguished in the midst of the darkness? And how can one be helped if this <term>order <note>original: "ordo"</note></term> puffs him up for a while with its empty wind and makes him into a Bishop of Laodicea, who cries out: "I am rich, and quite full, and need nothing!" when he is actually quite poor, miserable, blind, and naked despite all his perceived riches, light, and <term>theological apparatus <note>original: "Theologischen apparat"; refers to the technical tools, books, and methods of academic divinity.</note></term>? A friend is best recognized in a time of need: and so it must then be shown what kind of help and refuge one can have from and through this sort of thing, and what value is to be placed on such teaching. And thus, at the same time, it would be revealed whether one has more just cause to complain about their own conduct and their patron-gods, than they have to complain about those who are not well-pleased with them or who speak against them. All of this would easily and much more clearly be revealed if one were to take the trouble to dig a little deeper into the origin, nature, and fruits of this academic style of teaching and systematic order: for then, in its great poverty and deficient nakedness, it would stand as a shameful spectacle before everyone's eyes, and with all its old and new rags and tatters, it would hardly and poorly be able to cover its shame.

§. 3. For if one were to show this theology its true and actual origin, and remind it of its ancestry, one could point it nowhere else than toward Babel, to the mother of all confusion, whose language—and certainly not the language of <term>Canaan <note>A biblical metaphor for the spiritual language of the godly or the "pure" language of the Spirit.</note></term>—is spoken in these colonies in all sorts of <term>dialects <note>original: "dialectis"</note></term>. Now, the daughters of harlots cast this name far away into another land when they are asked where Babel is, and they point people toward Rome. But no one will believe them so quickly who sees the forehead standing before his eyes every day, where the mystery is written and who can well read such hidden script. Rather, it will likely remain the case that wherever the Whore rides upon the Beast, and the false prophet walks beside her and leads the bridle, there also is Babylon to be found—which well knows how to adorn itself and presents itself as a pure and holy Jerusalem and...

...be found. But who else is this harlot in her mystery but sin, which rides upon the beast, or holds its dominion within the man of sin and the self-will of the animalistic, beastly man? And who is the false prophet but one's own spirit and the carnal reason of the earthly-minded, who leads the natural man (who is already perverse enough) further astray with their earthly, human, and devilish wisdom? This wisdom comes from below, from the earth and the abyss, and can speak of Christ only in a beastly manner: just as their speech sufficiently betrays them.

For, dear reader, what is mostly found in those many <term>systems <note>original: "systematis"</note></term>, <term>compendiums <note>original: "compendiis"</note></term>, <term>positive theologies <note>original: "Theol. positivis"; refers to theology based on established doctrines and tradition rather than philosophical inquiry.</note></term>, and <term>academic lectures <note>original: "acroamaticis"; refers to technical theological instruction intended for advanced students.</note></term>, but empty letters—or if things are going well, all sorts of confused matters? It is a pervasive darkening and perversion of that which is clear, brief, and plain <note>original: "teutsch" (German); in this context, the author uses it to mean "plain-spoken" or "intelligible," contrasting it with academic jargon.</note> in itself, through the countless Latin <term>terms <note>original: "terminis"</note></term> and horrible-sounding words: <term>efficient causes <note>original: "causis efficientibus"</note></term>, <term>material causes <note>original: "materialibus"</note></term>, <term>formal causes <note>original: "formalibus"</note></term>, <term>final causes <note>original: "finalibus"</note></term>, <term>essences <note>original: "essentiis"</note></term>, <term>accidents <note>original: "accidentibus"</note></term>, etc. And for the rest, is there not an abundance of carnal zeal, <term>not according to knowledge <note>original Greek: "ὀυ κατ' ἐπίγνωσιν"</note></term>—that is, not according to inner recognition—and endless quarreling and strife? What is the cause? The teachers teach from divided hearts and have no fellowship of the Spirit among themselves, but are of different minds and disagree on the construction of their tower <note>A reference to the Tower of Babel (Genesis 11), symbolizing confusion and division.</note>. What one builds, the other tears down again: when one cries "Bricks!", the other brings lime; when one wants clay, the other brings stone. Meanwhile, every party, faction, and sect has its <term>systems <note>original: "systemata"</note></term> or <term>summaries of doctrine <note>original: "summas doctrinæ"</note></term>, <term>catechisms <note>original: "catecheses"</note></term>, and <term>institutes <note>original: "institutiones"</note></term>; and every one of them wants to be the best, the purest, and the most orthodox. Each appeals to Scripture and explains it according to their own orthodoxy. Thus they bicker with one another like harlots in a ditch, where one is as "pure" as the other, and they testify of themselves that they are altogether carnal, animalistic, and earthly-minded.

§. 4. If one were to treat this wisdom a little more gently and trace its rebirth back to another lineage, one still could not place it under any better heading than that of the **Papal leaven**. This leaven, immediately upon the occurrence of the **Reformation**, puffed up and soured the entire dough in place of the simplicity of **Jesus**, much to the deep concern of the good and quite differently minded **Luther**, whose theology did not smell of the professor's chair <note>original: "Catheder"; refers to the academic pulpit or podium of a university lecturer.</note> at all. Instead, interested parties perhaps took this falsely-celebrated art out of self-loving partisanship...

<meta>This page continues the "First Preface." The catchword from the previous page "lang-" combines with the start of this page to likely form the word "prolixity" or "complexity" (Langteylichkeit), referring to the dense, multi-layered nature of scholastic systems mentioned previously.</meta>

### First Preface.

<margin>*Balaeus in Iac. Cistert. p. 322.*</margin>
complexity as an **Egyptian robbery of Israel** <note>This refers to the biblical story of the Israelites taking gold and silver from the Egyptians upon their departure; Scholastic theologians often used this as a metaphor for "claiming" pagan philosophy for Christian use, a practice the author here critiques.</note>, and would gladly compare it to that with which the Israelites were later able to adorn the sanctuary and the Tabernacle of the Covenant. For it is the *Master of Sentences* <note>original: "Magister sententiarum"; referring to Peter Lombard (c. 1100–1160).</note> or "Master of Opinions," as he was called because he brought forth something new, who is only too well known as the author of this. He brought this style to its highest bloom and progress in his time, around the year of Christ 1140 under Emperor *Conrad III*, drawing it from the *Philosophy* of the heathens through the guidance and seduction of the teaching style of *John of Damascus*. Just as that man wrote four *books of sentences* <note>original: "libros sententiarum"</note> or opinions (just as <term>orthodoxy</term> <note>The author provides a polemical etymology here, suggesting that the word "orthodoxy" (right opinion) implies nothing more than human "opinion" or even "delusion" (Wahnsinn) rather than divine truth.</note> by the power of the word contains nothing else but opinions and delusion), in which he packed *Theology* together as if in a *compendium*. It was over these books—as the foundation of the entire *Theology* of the Papacy—that countless *commentaries* and glosses were later forged and smeared, and such writings were held even as equal to the Bible, if not higher. For following this *Peter Lombard*, who became Bishop of Paris in the year 1159, there immediately followed entire swarms of this kind of locusts that filled and flooded the land. These were so many "spirits of reason" and idle monks, some of whose leaders' names might be *Vazquez, Suarez, Molina, Fonseca, Thomas Aquinas, John Duns Scotus, Occam, Biel*, and other *most Aristotelian of Aristotelians* <note>original: "Aristotelicorum Aristotelicissimi"</note>, as a certain man (*) characterizes them not inaccurately. Indeed, entire sects of Summists, <term>Questionists</term> <note>Scholars who focused on debating specific "questions" or "disputations" in a highly structured, academic way.</note>, Albertists, Thomists, Scotists, Occamists, <term>Nominalists, Realists</term>, and others followed, by whom the dark Scholastic Theology—being more pleasing to them than any other—was set upon the throne.

Thus, even according to the testimony of modern Church writers, from the time of the Apostles onward, the Church has never been more heavily or cruelly plagued by bickering, disputing, strife, blasphemy, and condemnation...

# First Preface.

...look, then, at how little praise he gains from this; what can we do about it? It is certainly not our own invention that is being noted here, but merely testimonies from antiquity. Furthermore, these are mostly accounts that no one—not even those who have a vested interest in wishing they were not true—can reject or invalidate. And why do they appeal to such things, so that one must lay before their eyes what is otherwise not so well known? 

Thus, it is certain regarding **Augustine** <note>Aurelius Augustinus (354–430 AD), the Bishop of Hippo and one of the most influential Latin Church Fathers.</note> that he was not particularly fortunate in his conclusions and was no good **Logician** <note>original: "Logicus"</note>; consequently, he was also not good at **establishing** <note>original: "eruiren"</note> truths or creating doctrines and **systems** <note>original: "Systemata"</note>. This was despite the fact that in his youth he diligently studied **Aristotle** and possessed a sharp—though all the more unhealthy—reason, through which he could twist obvious **falsehoods** <note>original: "Falsa"</note> and uphold them as truth so that they had a deceptive appearance of reality. 

A single example may be enough to prove what we are saying: this is the accusation with which he charged **Manes** or **Manichaeus** <note>Mani (c. 216–274 AD), the founder of Manichaeism, a major dualistic religion that Augustine followed for nine years before converting to Christianity.</note>, claiming that he had passed himself off as the **Holy Spirit**. He based this on the fact that in a letter to **Marcellus**, Mani expressed the greeting of the Father and Son with these words:

-> **Grace, mercy, and peace, from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ!** <-

However, he did not include the **Holy Spirit**: **Therefore** <note>original: "Ergo"</note>, Augustine argued, Mani must have understood himself to be the Third Person of the Trinity. (†) 

But that is a perverse and absurd **conclusion** <note>original: "Ergo"</note>, especially coming from someone who was himself a **Manichaean** for many years and should have understood their teachings better—unless perhaps there was an even worse intention behind it, and he did not report it faithfully. Indeed, he did not depart from them out of entirely pure motives, but rather because they were not learned enough for him. 

One can also see from his writings how he dealt with the **Donatists** <note>A North African Christian sect that argued for a pure church and rejected clergy who had lapsed during Roman persecutions.</note>—a people who testified and campaigned greatly against the clerical estate and its corruption. Many of them may well have been better people than he became after he threw himself into disputing and quarreling and rose to high authority. One can see with what wretched and sophistical grounds he sought to overturn their teachings and confirm his own dogmas—as usually happens when partisanship and passions play the master and rule the pen. This is to say nothing of the many great errors in which he himself was stuck, according to the observations of the **Orthodox** themselves. If, therefore, the modern **systems** of those who rely on him for their way of teaching and **theology** are judged according to his **logic** and method—

# First Preface.

...sophistries, through which—following the impulses of blind reason—propositions were made and asserted regarding spiritual matters. This was also done by that Syrian monk and priest <note>Referring to John of Damascus (c. 675–749 AD)</note>, who was the first to prepare and concoct theology in a scholastic fashion using certain artificial propositions, <term>terms</term> <note>technical vocabulary</note>, philosophical rules of reason, <term>distinctions</term>, <term>limitations</term>, and personal opinions. §. 14. From these times, **Bede** <note>The Venerable Bede (c. 672–735 AD), an English Benedictine monk and historian</note>, who lived about a hundred and fifty years later, also inherited something, although he otherwise ranks among the most upright and pure of his time and is certainly to be regarded as a witness of the truth. §. 15. They call themselves **Evangelical** <note>A term used here to mean Protestant or "Gospel-aligned."</note> and put on a fine appearance, but for the most part, they are actually good **Aristotelians**; the Holy Gospel is far too lowly and simple for them, and likewise, **Moses** and the **Prophets** speak far too poorly—not "Academic" enough, as is the custom at Universities. > In the *Life of Luther* (Sheet 149. a. b.), it is recounted that Dr. Staupitz often thought of Dr. Summerhart, a teacher at Tübingen who dealt with his old scholastic and sophist teachings. ## First Preface.

...of academic teaching and theology itself, along with the books in which they are contained: while such textbooks, or the doctrine contained within them, ought to present a beautiful and noble necklace of pearls through their organization—adorned and shining with the most holy mysteries of faith—they look more like a rope braided from straw. And yet, the **Aristotelian-Pauline Doctors** <note>original: "Aristotelico-Paulini"; a critical term for theologians who attempted to harmonize the logic of the Greek philosopher Aristotle with the teachings of the Apostle Paul</note> boast of this, wearing crowns woven from these straw wreaths. They place everything in the intellect, so that their ornament and whatever makes them honored and respected is found entirely in their heads. 

In former times—before **Scholastic Theology** <note>A method of critical thought dominated by academic study and logic, often criticized by later reformers for being too dry and detached from faith</note> was brought forth again by **Lombard** <note>Peter Lombard (c. 1100–1160), whose book "The Sentences" became the standard textbook of medieval theology</note>—some evidence of divine things and Christian teaching could still be found in writings and books that possessed a certain flavor and the salt of wisdom. But now, in most of the largest volumes—which bear the greatest titles of "Master" and "Doctor" and are the most highly privileged—there is nothing but "dull salt," a **chaos of Christ’s doctrine and Aristotelian dregs, of all impieties the most execrable and blasphemous** <note>original: "chaos doctrinæ Christi & Aristotelicæ amurcæ omnium impieratum maxime execrabile & blasphemum"</note>, as one writer called it (*). It is a dark labyrinth of school-questions, **monsters of opinions, portents of words, scholastic tangles, horrid brambles** <note>original: "monstra opinionum, verborum portenta, tricæ scholasticæ, horrida senticeta"</note> (†), **sophisms** <note>clever but false arguments</note>, nonsense, foolish antics, empty doctrines, idle speculations, false traditions, school-deceptions, tasteless academic rowdiness, stubborn opinions, speculative religions, empty husks, straw, puffy water-bubbles, and **inflated voices** <note>original: "voces bullatæ"; refers to grand-sounding words that have no substance</note> and all kinds of wretchedly cobbled-together stuff; a brood of chimeras and other such "comforting" things. Yes, in a word: they are truly "empty food," from which any soul that has tasted even a little of God’s gracious Word and His friendly nature must rightly feel such disgust that they would shudder at it. 

Oh, the great misery and wretchedness! There are entire and great **bodies of doctrine** <note>original: "corpora doctrinæ"</note>; yes, indeed, mere bodies—**bodies without soul and spirit** <note>original: "corpora sine anima & spiritu"</note>—containing far less spirit and power for the building up of souls than is found in Cicero's *Hortensius*. According to his own testimony, **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), an influential early Christian theologian</note> was powerfully moved by that book, and he uses thoughtful words regarding it (††) which deserve to be quoted here. "That book," he says, "**changed my disposition, and turned my prayers to yourself, O Lord; it made my desires and wishes different. Suddenly all vain hope became worthless to me, and im-**" <note>original Latin: "Ille liber mutavit affectum meum, & ad te ipsum, Domine, mutavit preces meas, & vota ac desideria mea fecit alia. Viluit mihi repente omnis vana spes..."</note>

They were satisfied with the writings of the Saints and had no need for human art <note>The author uses "art" (German: *Kunst*) to mean the artificial logic and academic structures used by professional theologians.</note> to bring the divine teaching into order. Thus, for example, they hesitated for a long time to call the Holy Spirit "true God," or others to call the Son **consubstantial** <note>original Greek: *ὁμοούσιον* (homoousion), meaning "of the same essence." In this way, a pure life existed in the Church earlier than a precise knowledge of the Godhead or a **System of Theology** <note>original Latin: *Systema Theol.*</note>. According to the judgment of a sensible and wise man, <margin>(†††) Erasmus’s preface to Hilary</margin> the Church never suffered more damage than when it was thought she had gained something great through philosophy and worldly splendor. In former times, their greatest concern was that they all together, and each for himself, might be a **living letter of Christ**—written not with pen and ink, but with the Spirit of the living God, acting as the stylus of the "good writer" and the divine "court-chancellor." By this, they possessed the Spirit who taught them everything they needed to know and led them into all truth.

And how then could they walk in error? Could they not much more recognize and behold the same truth in its best order, **harmony**, **analogy**, **connection**, and the divine **Economy** <note>The "Economy" (*Oeconomie*) refers to God's orderly management and plan for the salvation of humanity.</note>? §. 43. Indeed, what shall we say? Even the so-called and manufactured **Canon** of Holy Scripture had its origin in this: it was an attempt to counter the excessive and free philosophizing and hair-splitting of "dark reason" which sought to gain the upper hand in the Church of God as grace greatly diminished. Because nearly everyone, following the blind counsel of their own perverse heart, sought to sell their own opinions, thoughts, and inventions as the Word of God and pure mysteries, great disorder arose in the Christian Church. Some well-meaning souls felt compelled by necessity to prevent this danger. Knowing no better counsel, they created a prescription <note>A standard rule or guide for belief.</note> for everyone to follow. Thus, they brought together various old copies of the Word, which had been spoken by the Spirit of God to the ancient saints in **Judaism** and to the apostles and disciples of the Lord!

### First Preface.

Concerning the Gospel on the Feast of the Three Kings <note>Epiphany</note>, folio 172a, he [Luther] speaks thus: No one invented the universities <note>German: *hohen Schulen*, literally "high schools," the standard term for universities in this period</note> but the devil himself, to destroy and obscure Christian truth, as has indeed happened, alas and alas. "From these murder-pits and hell-holes of all vice and impurity, people are then summoned to rule the churches—even when one wishes to call the very best and most capable to the task." "They are like," he says, "the Moloch <note>An ancient deity associated with child sacrifice by fire</note>, because therein the greatest and best part of the youth are sacrificed like a burnt offering." From these murder-pits (it says in another place **) emerge the locusts of Revelation 9 <note>In the Book of Revelation, locusts from the bottomless pit are a symbol of destruction</note>, which rule the whole world in all places, both spiritual and secular, so that even the devil, from the beginning of the world, could have devised nothing more powerful for the suppression of faith and the Gospel throughout the whole world than the universities. If one wishes to say that he spoke only of those under the Papacy—which cannot be proven—there is a passage in the Church Postil <note>A collection of sermons for the church year</note> (***) where he speaks of the very nature of universities, thus: The very essence of universities (for which "their schools" was later deceitfully substituted, so it would seem to apply only to the Papists' schools) is entirely an <term>offense</term> <note>German: *Aergerniß*; in a theological sense, a "stumbling block" or something that leads others into sin</note>, from the crown of the head to the soles of the feet, from the skin to the marrow, such that snow is hardly as much water as they are offense; and—take note—they cannot even exist without pure offense, since offense is their very nature and essence. Therefore, wanting to <term>reform</term> <note>German: *reformiren*; to improve or correct</note> universities—take note—while yet maintaining them in their essence, is exactly like trying to squeeze the water out of snow while still keeping the snow.

§. 58. But who can express this mystery of iniquity <note>A biblical term referring to hidden wickedness</note> and the abomination of desolation <note>A biblical reference to a great sacrilege that ruins a holy place</note> with words! None other than the Beast itself <note>Referring to the Beast of Revelation, often associated by reformers with corrupt religious systems</note>, in its own words, through which it speaks, reveals, and must make itself known, so that one may know who it is, and may judge it out of its own mouth and sentence it by its own words: which anyone who looks even with half an eye [can see]...

Meanwhile, the present writing and theology, which is here presented to the friendly reader, can sufficiently demonstrate the opposite—and show that we are no enemy of order in doctrine. It contains as much as may suffice for a system, and moreover maintains as good an order as the *Topical Works of Philip* <note>original: *Loci Philippi*; referring to Philip Melanchthon’s *Loci Communes*, the foundational systematic theology of the Lutheran Reformation.</note> or any others ever did. > What is born of the Spirit is spirit; and what is born of the flesh is flesh. <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 3:6.</note>

And that is precisely the difference between common School-Theology and that which is contained herein; such that a great gulf is fixed between the two, because they stand grounded in entirely contrary elements. And therefore it would likely be in vain to try to highly praise and recommend this writing to natural men, who stand under the rule of the flesh, since such flesh harbors and bears a constant enmity against **God** and His truth, and always lusts against the Spirit. For because the teaching therein is of **God**, it must—according to the proven judgment of Luther (*) —consider that it will be condemned by the greater part; especially by the clergy, prelates, and those we call the learned, as happened to all the prophets and apostles and to **Christ** Himself. But those who carry within themselves the testimony of **Jesus** and the Spirit of wisdom and understanding will surely taste what kind of food is being offered here, and it will surely taste good to them. For they will soon become aware of what evidence and power of the Spirit the testimony sounding forth here carries with it—even if it carries and gives off a wondrous and quite distinct language and tone—and how emphatically, indeed irrefutably, it legitimizes itself to the conscience of all men; so that on this account, there is no need at all to hang out a sign for good wine <note>A reference to the proverb "Good wine needs no bush," meaning that something of high quality does not need to be advertised.</note>. For what is never agreeable to the flesh—which finds no nourishment here at all—insinuates itself into the Spirit of its own accord, because it is truth, which [needs] our testimony...

# First Preface.

...and <note>Completing the thought from the previous page: "...writing here about such a matter as..."</note> one member owes to another through every joint, so that hearts may be joined together, and the body of *Christ* may be built up and joined together. Then let everything that is crooked, uneven, and unequal be made straight and level, and let all deceit, falsehood, and hypocrisy be put away, along with all envy and all backbiting, together with everything that disturbs, or can and will disturb, the unity of the Spirit! For what is a building without joints, and a body that is not directed into one another? Or can two walk together unless they are agreed? Or do we now first wish to choose the way of *Cain*? Do we not all belong to one Father, so that we are children of one race? Does not this nature and the new birth <term>Wiedergeburt: The spiritual rebirth or "being born again" central to Pietist theology.</term> bring with it that we should be loving toward one another as if by an innate impulse? Are we not also all baptized in one single Spirit into one single body? Oh, why then does one member act and position itself so strangely toward the other, just as if they did not belong together, or had no need of each other, or no care for one another?

Certainly, the anointing from the Holy One does not teach us this, dear brothers! Neither does the Spirit of truth lead us upon such paths; we have not learned this in the school of *Christ*; nor is the testimony of *Jesus* interpreted in this way: this is not how one follows the Lamb, nor keeps to the footsteps in which the *Lord* and Master himself walked: how then shall we lay down our lives for one another, if things go on like this? These are indeed no testimonies of the new birth, nor sweet grapes from the true vine, *Jesus*: this indicates no new name, nor does it bear witness of any transition from death to life: in this way the devil is not resisted, the world and the wicked one are not overcome: in this way the blood of the Lamb is not exalted in its power, and *God* is not called *Immanuel* <note>original: "Immanuel." Hebrew for "God with us."</note> in this manner: Thus one does not remain in the Father and in the Son, as *God* is in *Christ* and the Son in the Father: thus one also does not fulfill the joy and the will of *Christ*: Thus the coming of the day of the *Lord* is not hastened; nor does one enter into the rest of the *Lord* in this way: this brings no boldness <note>original: "Freymuͤthigkeit." A term often used to describe the spiritual confidence a believer has when facing God's judgment.</note> toward the day of judgment; indeed, one is rather easily put to shame on the day of the Lord.

§. 68. For we make no secret of this/ and you will surely find/ that no person of that sort—whose reason loves its own hypocritical holiness and righteousness/ which always wants to have something to touch/ to feel and to see/ which seeks something of divine service in forms/ figures and images/ and thereby becomes proud and puffed up/ yes, even perhaps presumptuous—will find anything advantageous for themselves here/ whether it be in times/ gestures or shouting/ in bread or wine/ in holy flesh or blood/ in baptismal water or the washing of feet/ or whatever else it may be/ in which the senses can take pleasure with devotion. For these witnesses leave nothing at all remaining for [human] nature/ but rather their way goes purely and solely into simplicity/ that is/ into spirit and truth/ and they lead beyond all images into a dark faith/ <note>"Dark faith" refers to a mystical state where the soul relies on God without the aid of sensory images or intellectual "light."</note> in which everything/ that is sensory/ must die and pass away/ or into that day/ when the elements/ and everything/ that is elementary/ must melt away with heat. Yet it is her own fault and her deserved reward/ that she be repaid and poured for twofold by the spirit of the two witnesses for all the heretic-making/ <note>Original: "Käkermachen" (likely a variant of "Ketzermachen"). This refers to the practice of labeling others as heretics as a means of persecution.</note> with which she has touched and persecuted the pure truth. ### ->Light and Life of Mankind.<-

Sects and factions <term>Rotten: a term often used pejoratively in this period to describe divisive religious groups or "mobs"</term> have been established among men: yet among them all, one finds none that actually prove in deed what they say and claim, or who do to others the good that they would wish to be done to them in every circumstance. This light judges and condemns selfhood and all these ungodly things or darknesses (under whose power the light suffers), as is, alas, plain as day.

Therefore, none of those who are caught up in this can testify in truth to the work of **GOD**, neither in its beginning nor its end. And this is finally the cause of damnation, which rests upon all those who are in darkness or outside the life of **GOD**.

# On True Faith.

[the] witness of truth, along with the light and word of Christ, is burdened and darkened. But the living faith sees in this light the one who is invisible <note>A reference to Hebrews 11:27, "as seeing him who is invisible."</note>, and holds fast to the **measure and portion of Christ and God** <note>The author uses "measure" (Maaß) and "portion" (Antheil) to describe the specific degree of divine presence or spiritual capacity granted to an individual soul.</note> that has revealed itself in his spirit. This measure of the Spirit is that which, through faith, daily works out the old and, in contrast, works in the new, both according to the will and according to the completion. The work of this divine influence is perfect, serving both to kill <note>In the sense of "mortifying" the old, sinful nature.</note> and to make alive.

But the powerless **worldly faith** is of a much different kind and is obtained thus: When someone hears a matter with their outward ears <note>Meaning physical hearing rather than spiritual understanding.</note>, and it is not unpleasant to their flesh—with which they consult closely and diligently for that reason—they then give their approval and rest there; and that is what the world calls "believing." This approval, however, occurs either according to the will of others or according to man's own will. The entirety of this so-called faith consists of mere **imagination, opinion, and personal conceit**. Just as human imagination, thoughts, and concepts change, so too does their faith change; it is entirely unstable—one way today, another tomorrow. Therefore, it cannot be steadfast because it does not stand in the measure and portion of God, as it is grounded and known in the hearts and consciences of men, which alone—like God Himself—is unchangeable. Because this faith is not from God, and God has no part in it, it also has no part in God and cannot please Him. This is a faith of the blind, indeed...

# On True Faith.

...a blind faith; for it cannot see the invisible, nor Him who is invisible <note>A reference to the spiritual sight described in Hebrews 11:27, "as seeing him who is invisible."</note>.

Because this faith also does not consist of that which strives against the world, and against the human will, and against the power of sin and the might of darkness—or is entirely opposed and contrary to all of them—it therefore lies under the human will and under the power of the **Prince of Darkness**, who rules and is active in this world.

But just as the world changes and the times shift, so too does this **worldly faith**. But as for leading someone upward out of the world and out of the changing times to the Redeemer of souls and to the Prince of eternal life—that it cannot do, and it is beyond its capacity. Thus, for all those who stand in the nature of this faith, the true living **faith in God**—which consists only in the divine <term>principle</term> <note>original: "principio"; here referring to the fundamental spiritual source or the essential beginning of a thing.</note> of a pure conscience—is a mystery and a hidden thing. For no one can accept the pure, true faith in God—which consists in Christ alone and is a pure gift of God—except in the spirit and the inner, new, and **reborn person**. In this, all those who have not been entirely emptied of this impure worldly faith have neither the slightest part nor any right.

Therefore, the faith of Christ and worldly faith are two vastly different faiths; they also have widely different effects and fruits that run entirely contrary to one another. The one believes in and confesses a freedom or liberation from the wrath...

# X.

## On Judgment or Sentence.

> The death and poison of the darkness are the day and the light /
> And for Satan’s kingdom of lies: the truth and judgment.

True judgment and sentence, as far as it has been recognized by man, is a pure gift of the Spirit of **Jesus Christ**, and is established and fixed by him in the heart and conscience of everyone who dwells or is found in that same light and life. It extends over everything that is contrary and opposed <note>Original: *conträr*. The author uses a Latin-derived term to emphasize the direct opposition between the divine and the worldly.</note> to the life and light of **God** and his Spirit. This divine sentence and judgment, as soon as it has been received and accepted by man, sprouts and grows more and more with divine authority, light, salvation, grace, and blessedness; it redeems the heart from all malice and impurity, and condemns everything that is opposed to the holiness and righteousness of **God**, so that **God** alone may be recognized and seen in the pure dwelling of his holy and undefiled temple. It is from there that he has promised that he would redeem Zion with judgment, and convert her with righteousness <note>A reference to Isaiah 1:27: "Zion shall be redeemed with judgment, and her converts with righteousness."</note>—yes, that he would cleanse and wash away all her filth with the spirit of fire <note>A reference to Isaiah 4:4, describing the "spirit of judgment" and the "spirit of burning" used to purify the faithful.</note>. ## XI.
# Of Perfection.

->Whoever wishes to deny a Christian’s perfection,<-
->Must first break them like a branch from the Tree of Life.<-

GOD Himself is perfection; therefore, all His works and gifts are also perfect: so that whoever receives His gifts, even in the smallest measure, receives that which is perfect; for nothing imperfect can come from Him. And through the receiving, enjoyment, and union with that very thing which is perfect, the creature <term>Creature|In this context, 'creature' refers to any created being, specifically a human soul.</term> is also brought to perfection. Likewise, the human creature can only be united with God, appear before His face, or be pleasing and blessed, to the exact extent that it stands in this perfection. 

But after the creature turned away and departed from that state in which it stood in the beginning—and in which its blessing and perfection resided—it fell into the Fall, the curse, and the deepest imperfection. As long as it remains in imperfection, it is still without redemption, grace, and Christ. For a person has no more and no less of Christ than he has of true perfection, because all perfection exists in Christ alone; and such perfection originates and flows from Him onto the members and fellow-brothers united with Him. Just as, conversely, all imperfection comes and arises solely and uniquely from the Devil. And these two are the highest opposites <note>original: *Contraria*</note> or most antagonistic...

## XI.
# On Perfection.

> He who would deny perfection to a Christian,
> Must first break him off as a branch from the Tree of Life.

GOD Himself is perfection; therefore all His works and gifts are also perfect: so that whoever receives His gifts, even in the smallest measure, receives that which is perfect; for from Him nothing imperfect can come. Since for these rulers, their law is their will alone, and their will is their law—while the written laws must serve only as a cover for their injustice—and since they know no other aim in their hearts than their own self-interest, they have at all times inflicted great suffering and tribulation upon the righteous. These righteous ones, for the sake of the fear of God and their own conscience, were not always able to bow beneath the rulers' corrupted will; indeed, those who have completely humbled themselves under the will of God in self-surrender <note>original: *Gelassenheit*; a central concept in German mysticism referring to the release of one's own will to become receptive to God.</note> absolutely cannot do so. And thus the rulers have laid the sword upon them—whom they should have actually protected—just as quickly, or even more readily and sooner, than upon the most unjust, godless, and wicked evildoers.

And thus, those who faithfully remained under pure fear and obedience <note>That is, obedience to God.</note> always had to endure shame, persecution, anguish, and sorrow from those who were outside His fear and obedience.

## Of Obedience.

> Whoever can rightly murder the **Basilisk** <term>Basilisk: In this spiritual context, a legendary serpent whose gaze was fatal, used here as a metaphor for the poisonous ego or "Self" that kills the soul</term> in his soul,
> Has become God’s obedient child in **Christ JESUS**.

Divine, spiritual, and living **obedience** does not consist of the ways, powers, and wills of men, such that men or women (according to the **old birth** <note>original: *alten Geburt*; a reference to the unregenerate human nature or "Old Adam" before spiritual rebirth</note> and **wisdom from below**) read the writings of the Saints, and—whenever they find therein what those Saints have done in the Spirit, power, and obedience of the Lord **JESUS Christ**—immediately set themselves to work to do the same in their **selfhood** and **conceit**. Through this **mimicry**, they achieve only a vain, false, and useless **copy** <note>original: *Copey*</note> of their own works instead of a true **original** of divine obedience. Nevertheless, they are anxiously troubled to set up and establish these copies in place of the works of Christ. Thus they obey their **own righteousness**, with which they imagine they cover and adorn themselves before God and men (even though such righteousness, by their own admission, is a **filthy and discarded garment** <note>original: *unflätiges und wegwerffliches Kleid*; a reference to Isaiah 64:6, describing human merits as "filthy rags"</note> that defiles and stains one however and wherever it is touched) instead of the **garments of salvation** and the heavenly ornament of the **righteousness of JESUS Christ**.

When, then, the person is raised up with their heart and mind out of the flesh—wherein shame and dishonor dwell, and which by nature is inclined toward mere vanity and dishonor—and is brought and transferred into the life in the Spirit, wherein the impure lusts of the flesh cannot be fulfilled; then the vessel of **honor** is begotten and prepared for the use of the honor of its **Lord** and Master. This vessel, while he (the human) still lived in and according to the flesh, stood ready, fit, and prepared only for dishonor and destruction, and knew neither its Master nor for what purpose it was meant to serve.

# Election of Grace.

<meta>catchword: Therefore</meta>

Therefore, **God** is not unjust, nor is He to blame for their destruction; rather, injustice exists and remains solely with mankind, as they are the ones who reject the holy, faithful, and profitable counsel of the **Lord**. Contrary to their own everlasting salvation—and according to the whims of their own perverse hearts—they choose to persist in that which **God** has eternally cursed, and in which all people (regardless of all their effort, work, prayers, and tears) must inevitably become obdurate and hardened.

Thus, the divine decree <term>Decree: (German: *Rathschluß*) refers to God's eternal plan or decision regarding salvation</term> certainly remains eternally firm and immovable: namely, that in this fallen nature—which is by its very kind opposed to **God** and all that is good—no one can be beloved or accepted before **God**, even if they were to shine with more virtue, zeal, and outward holiness <note>The original *Scheinheiligkeit* usually means hypocrisy today, but in this context refers to a "shining" or "seeming" holiness that is merely external and lacks the inner Spirit.</note> than all the children of **God**. For this is the apostate **Seed** <term>Seed: a central concept in Pietist thought, referring to the spiritual lineage or "nature" (either of Adam/flesh or Christ/Spirit) that governs a person's soul</term> in which **God** has placed enmity and opposition against His own Seed; therefore, it can certainly never be agreeable or well-pleasing to Him. For into this [apostate seed] He has planted His wrath and supreme displeasure; just as in the other [the divine seed] He has planted His highest grace and mercy, in which His soul also takes delight for the sake of His mercy.

According to this mercy, He also makes all those who live in that same [divine] Seed—and who allow it to rule within them—blessed through the washing of rebirth and the renewal of the Holy Spirit <note>A reference to Titus 3:5, a foundational text for the doctrine of regeneration</note>, which He has poured out upon them abundantly through **Jesus Christ**, the Savior. He does this so that they, being thus fully justified and pleasing to their **God** and Father, might become co-heirs of His grace, according to the hope of eternal life, which is certain and true.

# Concerning the Baptism of Christ

Where then is your calling <term>Beruff|A divine appointment or authorization to perform a religious office</term> to baptize? If you have a greater warrant from the "letter" <note>The author uses "Buchstaben" (letter) to refer to literal scriptural commands, contrasting them with spiritual authority.</note> for this than for the other, then you do well to show it, so that others may see it and regard you as the people you wish to be—and as those you try to persuade others you are. Because they thereby received the **Holy Spirit** and became partakers of Him, this proves to be a far different thing than being showered or sprinkled again with **water**.

Yet the words of Christ had to be fulfilled in this way! XIX.

## XXII.
### Of the Knowledge of GOD.

### XXVII.

## Of the State of Matrimony.

->Whoever wishes to give my soul its greatest title,<-
->Let them call it **God’s** bride, treasure, spouse, and life.<-

Although the state of matrimony <term>Matrimony: *Ehestand* in German; here referring to both the social institution of marriage and its mystical spiritual significance.</term> is known to all the world by name and custom, yet there are few who are informed of its mystery according to the foundation of hidden truth and secret divine wisdom. Nevertheless, everyone fancies themselves to be standing in a holy state of matrimony, even if they have begun and continued it in such an unholy and ungodly manner. They know, recognize, and understand no more of its foundation and origin, beginning and end, than perhaps a horse or a mule <note>A common biblical reference to Psalm 32:9, implying a lack of spiritual understanding or reason.</note>; instead, they live within it out of mere habit and according to the customs of the nations—or, at best, according to worldly laws—more out of compulsion and necessity than out of pure matrimonial love. 

The primary cause of this is that they do not know the **Lord**-Founder and Author of the same. But because they do not know Him, how then do they expect to know His mind, purpose, foundation, and will? And though they may seek to help themselves with the saying that the **Lord** spoke to **Adam**: *Be fruitful and multiply* <note>Genesis 1:28.</note>, this alone—without insight into the foundation and spirit in which and how **Adam** stood at that time—is truly not sufficient. Nor is it at all intended that every rogue <note>original: *Schalck* — a person of low character or a hypocrite.</note> and hypocrite, unbeliever and godless person, should multiply his malicious and cursed seed.

But whoever loves divine wisdom, truth, and knowledge, clings to them, and sows to the Spirit, shall be sustained in and by them, blessed and preserved from eternal destruction, and shall reap eternal life.

When all things are finally restored and brought out of the Fall and the disorder into which they have fallen, and are returned to the previous divine order, <term>Ordnung (divinely appointed arrangement)</term> it is necessary that first the deception, disorder, and the unrighteous carnal nature be made manifest. ## XXIX.

# Of Free Will.

> Nothing is stronger than God, yet He cannot prevent
> That I should not will and desire what I will. <note>This couplet reflects a common paradox in mystical theology: God is omnipotent, yet He grants humanity the agency to choose or reject Him, a concept central to the debate over "Free Will."</note>

In no way is a will to be considered or called **free** before **God** except for that which is entirely free from **sin**. And this is the very will which man lost in and through the **Fall** <note>The "Fall" refers to the biblical narrative of Adam and Eve's original sin in Eden, which many theologians of this period believed stripped humanity of its natural ability to choose good.</note>, when he admitted the will of the **Devil** and obeyed him; through this loss, man also fell into the **slavery** and servitude of sin.

However, everything—or as much as there is—that man knows and recognizes of **free will** in this fallen state is contained in that which struggles, moves, or sensibly proves itself contrary to the will of the flesh and the **Devil** within him, and is recognized and seen in the **Light of Christ**. <note>The "Light of Christ" is a key term for Radical Pietists and Quakers, referring to an internal divine spark or conscience that reveals sin and guides the soul toward God.</note> And this is the **will of God** in us, through which He desires our **sanctification**, but in no way the death and destruction of the sinner; which will of God, however, reveals itself only in and according to the **Spirit**. And just as this will is entirely free and always moves against the will of the flesh—which is under the servitude and bondage of the **Devil**—so it also ultimately makes free all those who obey it from the heart. And this is the free and liberating will, whose holy movements and presence in the **Spirit** and **mind** <term>Gemüth: a German term for the inner seat of thoughts, emotions, and the soul's disposition</term> are felt and experienced only by those who are turned toward the **Light of Christ** with all their heart. # To
## The God-fearing Reader.

->To all who mean, seek, and love the good and the truth with sincere and impartial hearts: Salvation, grace, and peace!<-

Since in these final, perilous times <note>The author uses apocalyptic language common to the late 17th and 18th centuries, reflecting a belief that the "last days" were at hand.</note> so many and various communities, religions, and sects, languages, tongues, peoples, and nations are found—each of which, for itself, with separate worship, understanding, and opinion, stands up for its own cause and religion to prove it the very best against all others—the whole world is divided into almost countless parts and factions. Each of these is, if not entirely, then for the most part, contrary and opposed to the others, as is sadly evident today. 

Because of this very godless and chaotic nature <note>original: "wüsten Wesens"</note>, which runs directly contrary to **Christ**, and the evils arising from it—such as hatred, blasphemy, strife, hostility (as is found among almost everyone), even murder and bloodshed, etc., and other ungodly and unhealthy things—I stand entirely impartial <term>impartial: (*unpartheyisch*) A technical term for those who sought a "true" Christianity outside of the established Lutheran, Reformed, or Catholic churches, refusing to take sides in theological disputes.</term> so as to have no part in such matters. Furthermore, in these sorrowful times, there has been granted to me by the highest **God**, out of pure, immeasurable mercy and grace...

# Appendix
## Poetic Verses. <note>The original title uses "Bedichte," an archaic variation of "Gedichte" (poems).</note>

### The Weight of the World.

The foam which the sea ever drives to the shore through storms /
Is light; a wing too, when the feather takes flight.
The chaff lifts itself up; a single hair scatters;
A reed is never heavy; no flax sinks to the depths.
Tender wool is light; of smoke there is nothing to say;
One knows the dust motes in the sun <note>original: "Sonnen Staub" likely refers to *motes*, the tiny particles of dust visible in a beam of light, a common Baroque symbol for insignificance.</note> / and whatever else settles.
The clouds also float, even those that carry fire within,
Which strikes out through a sudden crack with a loud bang <note>A reference to lightning and thunder breaking through the "fissure" of a cloud.</note> /
Even lighter than light: I shall name the shadow /
That is what the whole world with all its greatness shall be.
One will always recognize it as the lightest thing /
As long as false love adds its weight. <note>The poet suggests that worldly things only seem heavy or important when viewed through the lens of misguided human passion.</note>
What then is lighter, what more fleeting on earth /
Than bubbles that a child blows from a pipe for pleasure?
Which first must be dipped into wet soap:
It meets its end <note>Literally "gets the rest," meaning it bursts.</note> while still rising in the air.
But for one whom Love weighs—that love we hail as divine—
Then such a breath is far heavier than the world.
Do you wish to hear from my mouth what is lighter?
Let it be briefly known to you: Nothing is [lighter], for nothing falls more easily. <note>A play on words regarding the physical "fall" of light objects and the moral "fall" of nothingness/vanity.</note>

### The Poor World.

The false well is dry; not a single droplet of water springs forth;
The world, so full of itself, gives off a loud echo.
Love believes easily, and because it rings out so loudly /
And the world promises much, [Love] is everywhere deceived.
It rings with a strong sound, yet these are empty gifts;
The sound brings to light its innate emptiness: <note>original: "Lär," an archaic form of "Leere" (emptiness).</note>
The bells cry out that they have nothing inside them,
Just as a ringing barrel yields no wine at all. <note>In the Baroque tradition, a full barrel makes a dull thud, while an empty one rings loudly. The poet uses this to illustrate that the "loudest" worldly boasts are the most hollow.</note>

<meta>catchword: As</meta>

<summary>A collection of Baroque "Vanitas" poetry reflecting on the weightlessness and emptiness of worldly existence compared to divine love. The poems use natural metaphors like foam, dust, and soap bubbles to illustrate the fleeting nature of life.</summary>
<keywords>Vanitas, Baroque poetry, Weight of the world, Divine love, Emptiness, Worldly vanity, Metaphor</keywords>

# Appendix of Poetic Verses. <note>original: "Anhang Poetischer Gedichte."</note>

Just as hunger delights in food while dreaming /
And as the imagination often gathers treasures:
So too / even if Fortune has made you a master /
And honor / fame, and wealth / are credited to you /
You will find nothing outside the coffin <note>original: "Sär," an archaic form of "Sarg" (coffin). The poet suggests that once we die, the "empty world" offers nothing of value.</note> of this empty world,
When the night of the spirit vanishes before the day.

## Distinctive Avarice. <note>original: "Unterschiedener Geitz." In this context, "Geitz" (greed/avarice) is used as a metaphor for an insatiable longing, contrasting worldly greed with a spiritual hunger for God.</note>

When Israel there, freed from Pharaoh’s bonds /
Walked with uncertain steps through desolate places /
Where only hunger and thirst were present /
And where scarcity alone began to rule the household:
Then Heaven—I know not how—offered up food /
Through God's sweet gifts / prepared by angels:
Whatever the mouth craved / was immediately at hand /
Here, taste and scent / were provided for every dish.
Yet eye and ear found no pleasure in this /
The mouth still lusted after the style of other foods:
Although the senses lay soothed by delight /
Yet greedy Avarice is intent on strange fare. <note>A reference to the biblical account of the Israelites longing for the "fleshpots of Egypt" despite being fed manna from heaven.</note>
Even if the Ocean were to swallow all the water /
Thirst would find no rest from such a drink:
Fire does not forbid that one brings more wood /
The more that is procured / the more it craves.
What well can quench the thirst of the parched soul?
Ah, what rare delicacy soothes the mouth?
Avarice never has enough / how could that which is known /
Within the wealthy lap of the whole world ever fill it?
You alone / O Lamb of God! are my delicacy /
I hunger for You more and more / the more I eat of You!

## The Restless World.

The world revolves around itself in countless circles /
It follows itself / and flees from its own part.
Are you a man of war? How often is the hour
Of sleep spoiled for you by alarms in great haste:
If good Fortune does not diligently make its rounds /
No rest is found / to bring you to sleep.
A commander? If the whole army does not stand before you /
You feel no sleep / that stirs rest within you.

# Appendix of Poetic Verses. <note>original: "Anhang Poetischer Gedichte."</note>

The rich man / when space in the narrow barn is lacking /
For the abundance of his fruit / is not refreshed by sleep:
When but a tiny leaf rustles / because he counts his money
At night / then the greatest fear has ensnared him.
Although the dowsing rod <note>original: "Wünschels-Ruth." A tool used for divining or finding buried treasure, here symbolizing the elusive nature of wealth.</note> points to hidden treasures /
Yet your hand has not soon reached them both at once.
When shadow or light with a quiet foot climbs
Through the window into the chamber / then sleep is banished.
Therefore, that wise mind sensibly laughed
At the abundance of the rich / when fortune turned.
Hope / which intended to support itself through pleasure /
Stands firm only when placed upon God / rest is known in the Cross. <note>In Baroque literature, "the Cross" (Creuß) often signifies both the religious symbol and the earthly suffering that brings one closer to God.</note>
Should the world rest for you? It must not know itself /
And rise upon the Cross: then it can enjoy rest.

## Pride’s Shame and Reward. <note>original: "Hochmuths Schande und Lohn."</note>

IF fortune has elevated one through honor /
And placed them in the spot / where one feels the envious:
Let him not be proud of it / nor believe / that his well-being
Persists / when the people lead him with their wind. <note>The "wind of the people" refers to the fickle nature of public favor.</note>
Pride is only accustomed to bloating the insane:
Nereus's people <note>original: "Neris Volck." A reference to the sea-god Nereus; here, it likely refers to sailors or those tossed by the "sea" of fate.</note> make a merry farce /
When strong winds blow upon a fleeting ship /
And even the sail itself often wants to burst from its swelling.
Fortune / which is known for its fury among all ranks /
And has brought forth a reckless game out of malice /
Both gives the rule / and tears it from our hands /
Places one upon the throne / and also makes one despised.
Just as the joyful folk are accustomed to batting the balloon <note>original: "Ballon." A large, air-filled leather ball used in games, used here as a metaphor for the instability and "emptiness" of worldly power.</note> /
Which towers within, full of air and much wind;
Which must venture from the earth into the heights /
And nowhere, where it is, dwells in secure rest;
The ball has no rest / nor likewise do the powerful;
Pompey was a ball for the game of the round world /
(This is how balls are usually overtaken in a match) <note>original: "Duell," here referring to a competitive sport or game.</note>
He was felled by the executioner's hand / and indeed by the ax. <note>Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus (Pompey the Great) was assassinated and beheaded in Egypt after losing the civil war to Caesar.</note>
Honor filled Caesar with wind /
The Senate house was also stained by Caesar. <note>A reference to Julius Caesar being assassinated by senators in the Theater of Pompey.</note>
Marius was shrouded in as much sorrow /
As the many wreaths that were previously placed upon him. <note>Gaius Marius, a Roman general who held the consulship seven times but ended his life in a cycle of exile and bloody civil strife.</note>

When the people of Iapetus <note>original: "Japeti Volck." Iapetus was the father of Prometheus and Atlas; his "people" refers to the rebellious Titans or humanity in a state of pride.</note> there reached for heaven /
->And raised up castles / their construction was cut short:<-
Their desire / their evil deeds went to ruin /
->They were cast down from the heights with power.<-
Thus Lucifer / who was cast out from the number
->Of the stars / drew the throng of proud angels after him:<-
The joy of Paradise became distant to us ourselves /
->Because the first fall happened through the serpent's deceit.<-
After shame and mockery filled the high heavens /
->Sennacherib <note>An Assyrian king who besieged Jerusalem and was later murdered by his sons.</note> falls by the hand of his own people.<-
For seven years he had to bellow like an ox in the field /
->He who was known in Assyria and Babylon.<- <note>The author appears to conflate the fate of Sennacherib with that of Nebuchadnezzar, who was humbled by God to live as a beast (Daniel 4).</note>

# Appendix of Poetic Verses.

Pride also casts Antiochus <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes, a Hellenistic king whose persecution of the Jews led to the Maccabean Revolt; he is often cited in moral literature as an example of divine punishment for hubris.</note> into the pit /
After he stirred up great war and the abomination of the sanctuary.
Julian <note>Julian the Apostate, the Roman Emperor who attempted to suppress Christianity and restore paganism; tradition claims he was struck down by divine intervention.</note> dies / who exalted himself before God /
And spewed blasphemy / struck down by a thunderbolt.
Ah, fear the fall / you who tower yourselves so high /
And have proud horns / upon which your pride beats!
He remains not unpunished / who angers his God /
Who seeks out armor and weapons to wound Him.

## Solomon’s Petition for Wisdom.

With a thousand sacrifices Solomon presented himself
To the temple / when he wished to cry for favor and help;
When God desired of him a free wish in sleep:
Wish, O King! (He says) / it shall be pleasing!
Shall rich gold from the mine delight you?
Abundance will embrace you as a favored child.
Do you demand / that I should set you in honor here?
Two white horses are the lead team of your carriage.
Is this perhaps your wish / to count many years and months?
Nestor’s <note>A figure from Greek mythology known for his great age and wisdom; to "live the years of Nestor" was a common idiom for extreme longevity.</note> time and years do not match your time.
Will you choose Wisdom for yourself above all other goods?
Soon / soon she will offer her full breasts freely to you. <note>A Baroque metaphor for the nourishing and life-giving nature of knowledge and divine insight.</note>
Thereupon he pleaded for this grace / because God recognized it as good /
And took in the teaching of Wisdom with a full mouth.
When God grants you this / to which your mind turned /
Tell me / what will be left to wish for?
Let Midas <note>The mythical king of Phrygia who wished that everything he touched would turn to gold, which ultimately led to his starvation.</note> also let his words be heard:
Let whatever my hand touches turn to gold!
Let the years increase like Nestor’s time!
Let Euclio <note>The protagonist of Plautus’s comedy *Aulularia*, synonymous with a paranoid, miserly character who obsessively guards his wealth.</note> snore / who has brought in his goods!
Love binds all / one wish is not for everyone /
Because love itself makes such manifold wishes.
Proud love wishes for harmful goods to its own downfall;
Wise love strives after that / which brings true benefit.
One man wishes for property and goods / where nothing but fears rage:
But another loves that / where there is no evil cunning;
Prudence wishes to test its goods with a swift trial /
While Folly’s choice is like a sieve. <note>Meaning that Folly cannot retain anything of value, as it all slips through.</note>
Child / that you love wine and food / ointment / luxury and dancing /
The beautiful time of flowers and a long life!

# Appendix of Poetic Verses.

You who despise the arts / and wish to entrench yourself with Mars <note>The Roman god of war; here symbolizing a preference for violence and conflict over intellectual or creative pursuits.</note>
And say farewell to chastity for the sake of lewd passion!
Consider / that true goodness cannot delight you so,
Nor will heaven smile upon your perverse deeds:
Men will rank your foolish choice alongside ancient folly,
Which preferred stupidity over understanding and wit:
Therefore, choose virtue / no fairer possession can be found,
And prove it with the wise / so that wisdom may endow you!

## The Child-like Joy of the World.

A little child weeps here / and wets its cheeks,
Earnestly moistening its mother’s lap:
Yet here, the great sorrow is soon passed /
The bright clang of cymbals releases it from sighs.
What is childish can best soothe a child;
<term>Anticyran advice</term> <note>A reference to Anticyra, a Greek city famous in antiquity for producing hellebore, a plant used to treat madness. "Anticyran advice" refers to a remedy for folly or insanity.</note> / so worthy of mockery!
He is far more than a child / who by his own free will
Desires the ringing of bells over the throne of heaven.
Can a pipe gain more fame than Apollo’s harp?
Does a duck harmonize with the song of a swan?
They shall / as it seems to me / sport the ears of Midas, <note>In Greek mythology, King Midas was given the ears of a donkey by Apollo as punishment for his poor judgment in a musical contest; it is a classic symbol of ignorance and lack of taste.</note>
Being so displaced in Arcadia. <note>A poetic vision of a pastoral wilderness or paradise; the author suggests that even in a place of beauty, folly can take root.</note>
Heavenly music wipes away few tears,
For the harlot of the world purrs everywhere:
Though one might have a thousand reasons to weep,
Yet no tear is found / falling from the eyes.
Men know how to speak of nothing but dances,
Job on the dung-heap <note>A reference to the biblical Book of Job, specifically his period of greatest suffering and degradation; used here to represent the reality of human misery that the world ignores.</note> makes no impression.
Though hell and death wish to afflict you with fire and pitch,
Though you are already summoned before the Judge:
Yet because the harsh sound of the world has possessed you,
No misery / shame / death / or fire / can penetrate you.
Lust must return through some new sound,
Yes, even a mourning-song must be sung for the sorrow.
I fear / that joy shall be buried by sorrow;
In children, pain quickly wanes / and quickly waxes:
But not / where wit and virtue have their dwelling,
The highly-enlightened Spirit finds rest among the stars.
What is dearest here is that which renews heart and spirit;
For men / joy must always be manly too.

### Deceit and Fraud of the World.

When the sinful world <note>original: "laster-Welt"</note> wishes to court its favorite /
When she scatters her lure-bait / and is alert for the catch;
Then a cinnamon tree seems to blossom from her mouth /
What flows from her lips resembles a stream of honey.
Her sweet words one should value like gold /
Her blinking eye shines more than sunlight;
(Whose bright rays yet delight nearly everyone /
When her lovely face brings about a spring;)
Wherever she casts her gaze / there musk-roses grow /
(So believes the fool / whom she has enchanted / )
There one sees hyacinths and tulips caress each other /
There the whole world hangs full of bells <note>Reference to the "Schellen" or bells on a fool's cap, indicating that the world is a place of folly.</note> early and late.
This is her art / that she / like a vision / deceives /
Which shines through a faceted glass <note>original: "Rauten-Glas," a prism or magnifying glass that distorts and multiplies images.</note> from many corners:
You often count a thousand pieces / where barely a guilder lies;
The number comes from the art / through art it seems painted;
As many groschen <note>A common silver coin of the era.</note> as you see / so manifold is the shadow:
Thus deceives what through the world glistens as gold and golden.
Fraud is her art. When there had been filled
The chests of Crassus / <note>Marcus Licinius Crassus (c. 115–53 BC), a Roman general and politician often cited as the wealthiest man in Roman history.</note> his spirit rose;
He wanted to be Croesus / <note>The King of Lydia (r. 560–546 BC) renowned for his legendary wealth.</note> and hear nothing of Crassus:
Swap just two letters / then it becomes grass out of it. <note>A pun on the transience of wealth. In the poet's German wordplay, the name "Crassus" can be manipulated to "Gras" (grass), referencing the biblical idea that "all flesh is grass" and worldly glory fades.</note>
Gold can in deed and hope beguile everything /
That which the early and evening sun dries out through heat.
Meanwhile the world may count out so much to you /
So that she flatters you / until you become happy /
And gain a desire for her; yet you will find her lacking /
When you look for kernels / it is but empty oat-straw.
Her friendly face promises indeed beautiful gifts /
Yet in such appearance the false deceit is hidden:
Ensnared / whoever but bites: You can have an example
In the fish / who with its food also soon tastes its death.
Worldly love <note>original: "Weltlieb"</note> carries a net / whoever here runs after the world /
Will quickly himself be a prey of his own plunder:
Whoever looks for lust / and burns through the looking /
Runs / because he sees and burns / into that very net.

One stands before Virtue, the other before the terrors of the Flesh;
Here one is guided by toil, there by honor's gain.
The laurel-door <note>The gate to victory or fame, symbolized by the laurel wreath.</note> does not stand open to us,
Unless one has first made his way through thorns.
Much like the foreign style <note>original: "Welschen schlag," referring to Italian or French customs/games.</note>, when they strike the spinning top <note>original: "Kräusel."</note>,
So that it is set to run upon the smooth table.
Nor can one approach the golden ring,
Unless a proper key unlocks the door’s latch.
I indicate this herewith: let no one strive for victory
Who does not prove himself manfully in a difficult state!
That he might attain the palm branch <note>A symbol of peace and victory.</note> without any sweat,
And enjoy quiet rest without the toil of labor;
Or boast with sluggish feet at the Olympic race,
And know of fame and honor without a bloody struggle;
That he might possess the rich castle in Greece,
And attain peaceful rest amidst the Phrygian heat <note>A reference to the Trojan War; Phrygia was the region of Troy.</note>:
That he might win Lavinia <note>In Virgil's Aeneid, Lavinia is the daughter of King Latinus; winning her hand required Aeneas to fight a bloody war.</note>, yet without the heat of war,
Indeed, that the Italian realm <note>original: "Welsche Reich," here referring to the lands of Latium/Italy.</note> should come to the suitor just so:
That will not do: only the lazy man wants it thus;
Yet he shall have nothing: go forth and fight,
If you wish to be adorned with victory, honor, and gifts:
And if you will fight, then fight properly.

# Conflict of the Spirit and the Flesh.

They cannot dwell very well together in one heart,
The heavenly child and the earth-minded child.
No such grudge can seethe in Tantalus’s brothers <note>A reference to the bitter rivalry between Atreus and Thyestes, the sons of Pelops and descendants of Tantalus, who committed horrific acts against one another.</note>,
Nor from the Theban heat <note>The conflict between Eteocles and Polynices, sons of Oedipus, who killed each other in a civil war over the throne of Thebes.</note> can such a discord ignite.
This one and that one both carry artillery, arrow, and bow,
And fire upon us (though with a difference).
This one tips them with salvation, and that one with poison;
This one makes the chaste glow great, and that one, lust.
This one hates the darkness, and that one the sun's brilliance;
This one tears the night from our mind, and that one, the day.
Just as when a drop of milk dissolves into ink,
And the cuttlefish <note>original: "Sæpia" (sepia), referring to the ink produced by the cuttlefish, used metaphorically for clouding or darkening a clear situation.</note> is able to disturb the clearest river.
Chaste love is singed by foreign heat,
No less does the other shun the Acidalian glow <note>The "Acidalian glow" refers to the Fountain of Acidalia in Boeotia, associated with Venus and erotic passion.</note>.
Thus Wit <note>Reason or intellect.</note> and Downfall are set in long conflict,
Even Peace itself wages war against War in earnest.

Virtue cannot stand at all beside its opponent;
Life and Death never lodge together.
Here it leads you surely; there you must perish:
This one loves peaceful rest; that one wants to be armed.
This one fosters the virtues, and that one the waste of sins;
The key to both well-being and woe is assigned to both.
No greater well-being can be found in love,
Than what the fervor of Heaven bears here toward the lustful lecher.
Let there be one light for a world, a single love,
One King for one realm, and only one God of Love!
O God! let Your law of love be inscribed within me alone,
Let Your life be my delight; otherwise, let all else be dead to me!

## Nothing is without Suffering.

From the cross, the Romans took the Roman Law <note>Referring to the fact that Roman citizens were legally exempt from crucifixion, a punishment reserved for slaves and "low" people.</note>,
And only the servile were pegged to the vile wood:
No Roman nor free man has ever arrived,
Upon whose neck the yoke of the earth was placed.
We all must here, O world! bear your cross;
The overflowing of gall <note>A metaphor for bitterness or suffering.</note> brings no pleasure.
Pleasure itself nourishes and increases the plagues of the cross;
The cross breeds unnumbered crosses out of the cross.
Marble is too brittle for Sisyphus’s arms <note>Sisyphus was condemned in the underworld to roll a massive boulder up a hill for eternity.</note>,
The body is unfit for Ixion’s wheel <note>Ixion was punished by being bound to a perpetually spinning, fiery wheel.</note>:
The mouth cannot grow as warm as that of Tityos <note>Tityos was a giant whose liver was perpetually devoured by vultures; his suffering was legendary.</note>:
The thorn does not fit as well in the city of roses,
As the cross fits upon the world: why do you, delicate one, wish to flee
The cross, anguish, and hardship that stand fast here?
The snail cannot withdraw itself from its own shell,
Nor can a foolish man escape his own shadow.
Withdraw from the world and spread your wings;
The cross will simultaneously turn its thoughts toward Heaven.
Take the world upon yourself, as Phrixus once took the ram <note>original: "Phryrum"; refers to the Greek myth of Phrixus, who escaped over the sea on the back of a golden ram.</note>;
The heavy cross finds rest even upon the sea.
If you sit in full splendor as a guest at the King’s table,
The cross will be the first decider for you at the meal.
If you fall asleep, the cross makes itself a step
Of rest by your pillow, and settles in softly.
Soon the heart is bitten by envy and the tooth of Theon <note>original: "Theons Zahn," a Latin idiom (*Theonino dente*) referring to a malicious critic or backbiter.</note>,
And the mouth of Lycambes <note>Lycambes was a figure in Greek poetry driven to suicide by the biting satires of the poet Archilochus.</note> is set against the liver itself.
