Through worry without sleep our being must wear away;
Soon the heart is wounded by pain instead of claws <note>Likely continuing the metaphor of Tityos from the previous page, whose liver was torn by vultures.</note>.
Our limbs wish to pine away from illness /
Soon the foul frost creeps through marrow and joints.
Surely everything wishes to disregard Fabius <note>original: "Fabium." Likely referring to Fabius Maximus "The Delayer," a Roman general known for his endurance and patience.</note> /
And even out-shout the strong throat of Stentor <note>A Greek herald in the Iliad known for a voice as loud as fifty men.</note>.
For one, marriage <note>original: "Eh"</note> and for another, woe <note>original: "Weh"</note> has not turned out well:
Thus the cross within the cross is in love even with hope.
The ship makes the sailor / the seeds the farmer /
The wound [makes] the soldier / this saddens the captain.
The King’s cross is his kingdom / the gold of the rich [is theirs] /
One watches over the treasury / and the other the splendor of the throne.
Is it known to what end crosses signify a kingdom?
Why a great cross is placed upon coins?
The kingdom of the cross is great / the cross rules the world;
Should the world be defeated / let the cross be felled!

## The Soul Enamored with the Cross.

->Ignatius <note>Referring to St. Ignatius of Antioch (c. 35–107 AD), who famously wrote "My Love is crucified" while being led to his martyrdom.</note><-

### My Love is crucified.

->Only upon the cross alone<-
->Can Love <note>original: "Amor"</note> be secure.<-

Love stands firm at the cross: let the world and hell rage!
It will also be safe when it stands at the cross.
Thus a house laughs at every storm if it has its place
Upon Olympus <note>The mountain of the Greek gods, here used as a metaphor for a place of divine peace above earthly weather.</note> when the north wind blows.
The cross is rock and house, if you can reconcile yourself to it,
Only love Love and usefulness: love stands firm!
Fortune’s wheel <note>original: "Glücks-Rad"</note> may shift the world countless times,
Just as a small ship <note>original: "Schiffgen"</note> lets itself be turned in the whirlpools;
As a spinning top <note>original: "Kräusel"</note> goes faster on the plain,
And a wheel more fleetingly when winds drive it on:
Love stands firm / Fortune stands at the service
Of Love / which cannot be brought to a fall.
Even if the greatest need strikes with a thousand blows,
It considers the blow a joke and the stroke a pretense:
When anxiety lays a strong bond on hands and feet,
It thinks that it is good for foot and hands.

Hunger's tooth gnaws / the fire of thirst faints;
   No hunger or thirst can harm love.
Naked she wanders through the world / risks shipwreck / and observes
   The need and danger of death / the cunning of earth and sea.

   Let the tyrant be Maxentius <note>original: "Maxentz." Maxentius (r. 306–312 AD) was a Roman Emperor often portrayed as a cruel persecutor in Christian literature.</note> or Nero;
Let him stoke the fire / and reach for his sword:

The executioner may swing the ax with strong arms,
   Love goes unhesitatingly into the face of death.
Death brings delight. You shall struggle for salvation and hope;
   Love has fixed hope and salvation upon itself.
Suppose a thunderclap should rise from heaven;
   Let virtue itself gather its strength;
Let the thunder strike / let hell be moved;
   Let the old and new world also consider this:
Love will yet endure, so long as the Cross stands;
While all pain vanishes through the glow of heaven!

## Contemplation of the Love of God in Christ Jesus revealed on the Cross.

God's love undertook everything for our sake /
   And sought the world through fear and hope,
Which yet remained hardened in its mind as before /
   Nor was it mastered or set right through word or punishment.
Look upon this last thing: Cross, nail, thorn, and pillar /
   Rope, scourge, spear, and reed / anxiety, love, sweat, and blood!
I know, it takes away the lust of sin / the rot /
   At the Cross the world becomes fit for heavenly love.
Should a golden crown then adorn your brow here /
   And a thorny one stand upon God’s head?
Do you want the scepter? Shall God carry a worthless reed?
   Is His place a rock / your seat ivory?
Does His own blood dye Him / and the snail-purple <note>original: "Purpur schnecken." Tyrian purple, a dye derived from sea snails, was the most expensive and prestigious color in the ancient world, reserved for royalty.</note> dye you?
Does a white robe <note>original: "weisses Kleid." Referring to the robe placed on Jesus by Herod Antipas to mock him as a fool (Luke 23:11).</note> shame Him / while it bestows honor on you?
Should the golden chain cover you / and only iron cover Him?
   Is God then imprisoned / and you [dressed] in jewels?
Are you surrounded with goods together with your house /
And live in abundance / dwelling in the upper city:

## The Changed Heart.

Triumph! Wisdom now dwells within the heart,
Love conquers, the world's path is entirely blocked off.
Through pleas, money, violence, through power, through cunning, through jesting,
You, o false world! shall not be brought into the heart:
Even if the sphere of the earth turns to rain of gold,
Through which, as they say, Danaë's <note>In Greek mythology, Danaë was imprisoned in a bronze tower, but Zeus reached her by transforming into a shower of gold. The poet uses this to show that even the greatest worldly temptation cannot reach a heart devoted to God.</note> chastity fell.
A heart united with God cannot be conquered,
Because it has unlearned the world's buffoonery <note>original: "Possenspiel." Refers to the deceptive, theatrical antics of worldly life.</note>:
Since it has felt the danger and the hook,
And tasted the juice of gall in the mouth of pleasure.
The Heart has stolen holy Love away from the [worldly] heart,
And hidden the impure flame within a chaste glow.
Therefore it grasps the pure heavenly flames with desire,
So that only the heavenly good from above may enter:
The heart is by nature only entirely closed at the bottom,
But not at the top, so that it may stand open to God. <note>A common Baroque emblem: the physical shape of the heart—pointed at the bottom and wide/open at the top—symbolizes that it should be closed to the narrow earth and open to the vastness of heaven.</note>

## Main Summation.

As my spirit soars to the high thrones of heaven
From the hollow and prison-house of my body,
It happens that the trifles <note>original: "Tand." Refers to worthless, flashy trinkets or worldly vanities.</note> of the vile world stink to me,
And I no longer desire to dwell in this house of mourning.

## Entrance.

The soul, which the fire of heaven has ignited,
Burns toward eternity with a bright flame,
And turns back to Him from whom she first originated.

---

He who is united with JESUS through the bond of love,
Sets the goal of his hope only in the field of heaven,
And has long since wept for the vain trifles of the world,
Which an earthly man otherwise takes for pure honey.
One sees how he who has once burned himself in the fire
Flees the hot flames with well-considered fear,
And is not presumptuous, nor runs through the embers,
Nor pulls a glowing plate of metal through his fingers. <note>A metaphor for avoiding the "heat" of worldly temptations or the painful consequences of sin after having been once "burned" or enlightened by God.</note>

Since misfortune flowed to us from the apple /

Which so seduced man through the apple /

Which are all infected by one spirit / the **Devil**;
Look at yourself wherever you will, and one will peep out!
Be it a **Dog / Peacock / Goat / Sow / Donkey / Ape / Lion / Dragon**, <note>In the devotional literature of this era, animals represented specific sins: the peacock for pride, the goat for lust, the dog for envy, etc.</note>

Born from above in the manner of Christ’s Spirit:
Toward this, O Man, direct yourself / and believe the Savior’s oath!
For flesh and blood are of no use / the old is lost,
What comes from heaven / goes only to heaven now.

## Lament over the Fall of *Adam*.

Ah! Who will give my head enough mild water,

## The Deceitfulness of the World.

Even if I surpassed Methuselah <note>A biblical patriarch said to have lived 969 years; used here as a symbol of extreme longevity.</note> in years,
And if Suada <note>The Roman goddess of persuasion and eloquence.</note> herself had taught me the art of rhetoric:
Even if I had experienced ten times more than Ulysses <note>The Latin name for the Greek hero Odysseus, renowned for his cunning and his ten-year journey home from Troy.</note> of old,
Even if Minerva <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom.</note> herself bestowed her wisdom upon me:
Still, my lips and tongue would fail me:
My understanding, mind, and courage would vanish,
If I were to fully express the world’s deceit,
And overlook no part of the foundation of her falsehood.
For when she acts friendly, she burns with anger and zeal:
When she speaks of honey, she prepares poison.
When she speaks of love, she foams with the bile of envy:
Whoever her speech touches is already half lost.
For her words are set snares,
With which whoever trusts her is brought to ruin.
Through poisonous, cunning appearances, she can compel the senses:
For whomever she even looks upon, she has already crafted a net.
Therefore, flee from the world! She has swift arrows;
Whoever comes too close to her will be mortally, harshly wounded.
Whoever believes her cosmetics <note>original: *Schmincke*. This refers to the deceptive "makeup" or false facade the world puts on to appear beautiful.</note> feels her thunderbolts;
She has set her target on the one who hardly thinks of her.
Whomever she wishes to raise to great honor and high status,
She has destined for bitter shame and a deep fall.
To the one she bids live in sweet pleasure and joy,
She has prepared a wormwood-mush <term>Wormwood: A plant famous for its extremely bitter taste, frequently used in literature to symbolize bitterness, hardship, or medicinal punishment.</term> and a gall-drink.
To whom she gives many treasures and rich gifts,
She has already prepared the beggar’s staff <note>A symbol of total poverty and destitution.</note>.

Therefore, do not trust the world! She loves and then she grieves;
Her sweet honey is soured with poison and gall.
The false crocodile devours you with wet eyes; <note>A reference to "crocodile tears," an ancient belief that crocodiles wept while eating their prey to lure or simulate sorrow.</note>
Venus kills you, even while her mouth laughs. <note>Venus here represents carnal desire or worldly beauty.</note>
The soft world washes with a sharp lye;
Whoever seeks freedom from her has made himself a servant.
Therefore, do not trust appearances; do not let the glint lead you astray!
He who is easy in belief is also easily led astray.
He who is untrained can soon be confused:
He who is all too certain has been touched by Circe's curse. <note>original: "Circens Fluch"; referring to the enchantress Circe from Greek mythology who turned men into swine.</note>
Ah, people, take heed, rouse your senses,
And recognize the world’s trifles with watchful eyes!
He who wishes to escape her wide net with prudence
Must provide himself with wit <note>In this 17th-century context, "wit" (Witz) refers to mental sharpness or intellect rather than humor.</note> and must not be overconfident.
But he who rushes toward her yarn with thirsty desire,
And hangs himself on her hook out of lack of understanding;
He has pinned himself with force to her stake,
And already sunk body and soul into the abyss-pool.
Pull me powerfully away from here, my God, through Your love,
And lead my spirit into the kingdom of eternity:
Let me always be with You with heart and all senses!
With You is quiet rest; here is sorrowful strife.
And help me, as long as I must still wander in this world,
That I may stand on constant guard and good watch:
So that the enemy's army may not ambush me,
And I might not perish out of overconfidence and unexpectedly!
If the power of hell then comes and wishes to strongly contend with me,
So let me go out to meet it with a brave spirit!
I will nonetheless tread the field in Your strength,
And after the desired victory, strive through the struggle.
Yet Lord! from You alone comes whatever good we have:
If I am to enter the battle, then You must grant me shield and sword
And bow, and refresh my weary spirit.
Give this, Lord: that is what Your poor servant now desires!

And aims at me with misfortune full of cunning,
So that I do not do what harms and injures me,
And I, fooled by appearances, disturb my own peace.
When she sets a beautiful net for my feet,
And lures me with sugar, which is yet embittered with poison,
Then overthrow her, my God, in a swift moment!
I want only to hang upon Your hook, <note>While being "hooked" usually implies a trap, the poet here uses it to mean being safely caught by God's grace to avoid the world's deadlier traps.</note>
And press through the flood of waves to Your lure:
For with You, my goal of hope will not be shifted;
Nor will I ever be deceived here by false appearance,
Ah no! whomever Your love has drawn into its net,
Has found what refreshes him here and eternally there.

### IV.

Through a perverse game and vain practice,
Excited by pale envy and empty love,
The hearts and foundations of all men are moved,
And the very globe of the world is driven around in a whirlpool.

## Destructive Self-Love.

How blessed was the time when our senses were not yet
Conquered by "mine" and "thine," <note>original: "mein und dein"; a common philosophical phrase referring to the invention of private property, which many 17th-century thinkers blamed for the end of human harmony.</note> when no property,
The dungeon of true peace, could win us over,
When the flower of beautiful freedom still bloomed in simplicity:
When one was content in quiet pleasure with that
Which heaven, earth, air, and sea gave in common;
When one did not yet war anywhere with bitter wrath
Over what neither wants to nor can be another's slave:
When he whom one called King was yet nowhere to be found,
When everyone was their own lord and king:
When [the knowledge of] how one should oppress or fleece one's neighbor,
And the "art" of our nobility, was not yet manifest. <note>A satirical remark suggesting that the "skill" of the upper classes consists largely of exploiting those beneath them.</note>
Where have those times gone? Where have they vanished to?
So that now one knows not even the smallest trace of them.
Instead, self-love has now arisen,
Which tears into a thousand pieces that which freedom bound.
To one his house is too small, and to another his land too narrow:
This one begrudges the other what heaven gives him:
That one wishfully desires a beautiful, grand display:
This one a neighbor's luck has dismayed and saddened.

### IV.

Through a perverse game and vain practice,
Stirred up by pale envy and vain love,
The heart and the depths of the senses of all people are moved,
And even the orb of the world is driven about in a whirlwind.

## Destructive Self-Love.

How blessed was the time when our senses were not yet
Constrained by "mine and thine," when no property— <note>original: "Eigenthum." The poet is mourning the loss of a legendary "Golden Age" where everything was shared in common.</note>
The dungeon of true peace—could win us over;
When the flower of beautiful freedom still bloomed in simplicity:
When one was content in quiet pleasure with that
Which heaven, earth, air, and sea gave in common;
When one did not yet wage war anywhere with bitter fury
Over what neither wants to be nor can be another's slave: <note>Referring to the elements of nature (air, sea, sun) which cannot truly be owned.</note>
When he whom one called "King" was not yet to be found,
For everyone was their own master and king:
When how one should oppress or fleece one's neighbor—
And the "art" of our nobility—was not yet revealed. <note>A biting social critique suggesting that titles of nobility and the "art" of ruling are merely sophisticated ways to exploit others.</note>
Where have those times gone? Where have they died away?
So that now not even the smallest trace of them is known.
Instead, self-love <note>original: "Eigen-Lieb." In this context, it implies egoism or selfishness.</note> has now arisen,
Which tears into a thousand pieces what freedom once bound together.
For this man, his house is too small; for that man, his land is too narrow:
This one begrudges the other what heaven gives him:
This one longingly desires a beautiful, luxurious display:
That one is dismayed and saddened by his neighbor's good fortune.

That one had to endure hunger and thirst before eating wine and food;
   Sweat and worry were called his rest; the conflict was never far.
Even He, by whose word the stars stand still,
   From whom all well-being, wealth, and honor flow,
Is miserable, naked, and bare (this was the Father’s will),
   Journeyed toward heaven by a bitter step. <note>original: "sauren Tritt." In 17th-century German, "sauer" (sour) often carried the connotation of "hard-earned," "painful," or "laborious."</note>
A sharp thorn first crowned His temples
   Before the proper crown came upon His head:
The scepter, which now the sun’s radiance beautifies,
   Was once a humble reed that His hand took up.
A black discharge <note>original: "schwarzer Eiter." Baroque poetry often used graphic imagery of Christ's physical suffering to emphasize the magnitude of His sacrifice.</note> first came from His wounds,
   From which now much radiance shines with a thousand suns.
Patience is the path to the palms: <note>Palms are a traditional symbol of victory and martyrdom.</note> whoever has felt a desire
   For them, never turns away from the rough road.
But it did not suit that one who also sought palms,
   And asked the Crucified One to be his heavenly guide:
When he heard that He made him a stranger <note>A reference to the biblical story of the Rich Young Ruler (Matthew 19), who was told to give up his possessions and follow Christ.</note>

O heavy burden of the world! he would much rather forfeit
   God and heaven itself, than just the appearance of wealth.
Not so are those minded whom virtue has elevated,
   And whom the hot glow of heaven has proven:
Moses and Abraham are witnesses of such trials,
   And the host of Apostles experiences this likewise.
The one had to leave his land, the other his house, and all these;

And these taught the world on every street,
   And their law is valid in heaven just as it is here.
You, who now love that place where vice never hovers,
   And only regard the joy that no fear violates,
Mark and consider well what teaching they give!
   In word and conduct it is said: We are appointed to the Cross!
This is the glory of the saints; with tribulation, bonds, and lashes
   They parade: <note>original: "Stolziren." The poet suggests that the saints wear their scars and chains like badges of honor or fine clothing.</note> how can this be? It comes from a good hand.
Do you think it signifies hate? No! they are signs of love:

No one climbs in triumph to the peak of the Capitoline <note>original: "Capitoles spitze." This refers to the Capitoline Hill in Rome, the destination of a "Triumph," the ceremonial procession of a victorious general.</note>
Who has not first bravely dealt damage to the enemy:
Through nettles, prickles, thorns, through cliffs, the heat of fire,
Through hard-frozen ice, through high-snowy paths,
Yes, in the midst of battle, through wounds and through death,
Virtue climbs to the Heavens <note>original: "Pol," meaning the celestial pole or the highest point of the sky.</note> by the narrow path of Hercules: <note>A common Baroque reference to the "Choice of Hercules," where the hero chooses the difficult path of Virtue over the easy path of Vice/Pleasure.</note>
Nothing without effort; one must earn joy through pain:

But you will have a prize by forsaking the world,
The likes of which falls to no one at the Olympic Games: <note>original: "Olymp'schen Kampff." The poet compares spiritual renunciation to the highest earthly athletic achievement.</note>
So hurry, and spit it out! <note>Refers to the "bitter world" or worldly vanity.</note> He receives the gifts of victory,
And possesses the most, who cares nothing at all for the world!

## The Pure Foundation.

Whoever strives for sweet honey in the bitter world,
And seeks the delight of Eden in a field of thorns,
<note>fleuron ornament</note> Has cursed himself to harm upon a stray path,
And stuck his horn of salvation <note>original: "heyl-horn." A biblical metaphor for strength and protection (Psalm 18:2).</note> to hard ice.
That which floats upon light vapors without a firm foundation,
Cannot be my dwelling nor my soul’s anchor:
That which only gleams with a painted shine in a distant place,
Is not that in which my spirit and soul now live.
The ground upon which my mind and spirit now rest,
Must be such a rock that is untouched by Time. <note>original: "den keine Zeit beschmückt." Literally "which no time adorns," implying it is eternal and does not change with worldly trends.</note>
Therefore, would You, my God, break the false foundation
Which the evil world deceitfully placed beneath me,
And as a thing of no value, destroy and pierce through
Every appearance that does not hold true colors!

## VI.

The vain world cannot equal Heaven:
Even when its proud spirit mingles among the stars,
Its false brilliance is nonetheless mockingly wiped away:
For when the sun shines, the moon must surely turn pale.

## The Valued World.

What God and Nature have placed in worthless dust,
And sunk into the deep sea of unworthiness;
And what the very nature of the thing itself destroys,
Cannot by any right be hung in the House of Fame. <note>original: "Fameus Hauß." An allegorical reference to the dwelling of the goddess Fame (Rumor), where the deeds and names of people are displayed to the world.</note>

An old, rusted steel must surely give way to gold;
A hideous rag is not esteemed as velvet is:
A pebble cannot reach the value of a diamond;
And a cheap **baize** <note>original: "Boy." A coarse, napped woolen fabric, often used in contrast to the luxury of silk or velvet.</note> does not equal the splendor of **purple**.
What is world and worldly / cannot call itself heavenly;
A shining **comet** <note>In the 17th century, comets were often seen as fleeting, ominous "false suns" or portents, unlike the steady light of the sun.</note> is not the sunshine.
One soon learns to know the bird by its song;
The little **shrew** must be its own betrayer.
Even if an **Absalom** <note>The rebellious son of King David who attempted to usurp the throne of Israel.</note> wants to rule **Israel**,
And strives for kingdom and crown with a steeled arm;
Yet only **David** must lead the **scepter** successfully:
For he alone is high / whom **God** raises to honor.
World! do you dare, with your **childish toys**,
With your trifles / to step into the light of day?
Will you make your **shadow-play** equal to the light of Heaven?
Shall **Time** stand in equal balance with **Eternity**?
Look / at what the Devil does! A wasted skeleton,
A long-decayed carcass of the dead world,
A dark valley of death likens itself to the highest cliff,
To high **Eternity** / into which no shadow falls.
Where a daring troop has conquered the power of the senses,
And proud **presumption** <note>original: "Aberwiß." A Baroque term for a misplaced, over-clever, or mad sort of pride/wit.</note> has filled the hearts:
There the poison of Hell has also forced its way in,
And shrouded the light of the mind with thick night.
Therefore the foolish world comes with **absurd things**,
Which rest only on a light wind and empty mist;
And wants to bring counterfeit goods to the market,
And pass them off at high value, just like the valid ones.
Yet he whose eyes are not yet entirely blinded,
Can soon see the light snow of false deception.
But he who has turned his mind only to the appearance,

Do not let your understanding melt away like wax /
Which a warm air soon lifts from its solid state!
If the wicked world wants to delude you with false appearance /
When she comes with brilliance in her **snake-skin**; <note>A common Baroque metaphor for the world’s deceptive beauty, appearing shimmering and attractive while hiding a venomous nature.</note>
Then let Truth also hear the firm foundations /
Upon which she [the world] boldly builds her great boasting!
Ah, truly / as the chaff cannot remain before the wind /
And as the fire quickly consumes the rest of the stubble:
So a wind from the Lord will scatter the smoke of the world /
And what smells of earth / will be overturned.
Lord / teach me to distinguish the appearance from the essence /
And instruct me / what is the **kernel** and what is the **shell**! <note>original: "Kern und Schaale." A recurring motif in 17th-century German literature, emphasizing the spiritual reality (the kernel) over the outward, material form (the shell).</note>
So that with understanding I may avoid the world’s cunning /
And flee her deceit and poisonous hypocrisy.
Not what glitters from the outside shall conquer my spirit /
Nor shall vain clowning master my mind.
Only Your truth / Lord! shall penetrate my heart:
Whatever separates me from this / take graciously away from me!

## The Soul Does Not Trust the World.

Lord! when the world wants to paint me a kingdom of heaven /
While she prizes her appearance as equal to a good essence /
And with daring defiance impudently sets herself at the side;
When she wants to boast presumptuously with empty air /
And pay with **glazed clay** <note>original: "verglaßtem Thon." Likely referring to lead-glazed earthenware that mimics the shine of more precious materials, used here as a metaphor for "counterfeit" spiritual value.</note> as if it were good coin;
Then let me walk carefully out of the way of her deceit /
Let me look only for Truth with burning love!
Thus I always take the kernel over emptied shells:
Her poisonous snare shall not be harmful to me /
When Your wisdom gladdens me with help.
Therefore I pray / let her [Wisdom] always dwell in my soul /
That she may be my **lighthouse** <note>original: "Pharus." Refers to the Pharos of Alexandria; a common term for a guiding spiritual light or beacon.</note> and the light of my senses /
According to which the mind’s **compass** and needle are directed /
When now the storm of the world will not spare my ship.

### VII.

Now that my mind feels the agony of the night /
I notice / that I am more than a servant and a slave /
And I sigh: stand by me / O eternal light! /
Until my seduced spirit finds the way of life.

## Repentance of a Penitent Soul.

Cursed be the day that chose me for this /
->To be a firm target of vanity!<-
The hour in which I lost what was uncertain /
->To lack the beautiful sunshine forevermore!<-
The man who afflicted my neck with this yoke /
->And led my poor heart into vanity,<-
May he be worthy of a millstone sinking him into the sea / <note>A reference to Matthew 18:6, where Jesus suggests it is better to be drowned with a millstone than to lead a "little one" into sin.</note>
->And receive his reward, as he justly deserves!<-
My God! I feel now the sharpness of Your arrows:
->When Your hand of wrath presses one as it does me now,<-
He feels how Your grim fury and hard thunderbolts
->Pluck the sin-filled soul into the abyss of Hell.<-
The days of my time have for the most part flowed away /
->The pointer of my years stands already near the end:<-
They have shot away in rapid haste like a stream /
->And my evil works stand there before my eyes.<-
O God! the judge within the conscience now stands up /
->What my eyes see intends to be an accuser against me.<-
I am beaten and torn from foot to head /
->And suffer miserably almost the heavy pains of Hell.<-
What my perverse heart previously delighted in /
->Now earnestly reproaches me for my evil deed:<-
What placed me in contentment and sweet pleasure /
->What most of all delighted me before,<-
Appears as an avenger and torments my senses; <note>original: "henckert," meaning to act as a hangman or executioner; here, the guilt acts as a torturer of the mind.</note>
->O faithful God, shall I perish in this anguish!<-
What shall I, poor soul, begin in such distress!
->Can no helper and no savior then be seen?<-
O God, do not cast away the one whom You once made—
->Like Manasseh and other sinners—righteous and pious.<- <note>King Manasseh of Judah was a biblical figure often used in 17th-century literature as the ultimate symbol of a great sinner who was forgiven after a profound, humble conversion.</note>
Let me also embrace Your help like the others!
->Let me be regarded as a servant by You through grace!<-
Indeed, the multitude of my sins surely exceeds
->The small grains of sand in the sea, the dust-motes in the air:<-
Yet let me, a poor servant, still find grace with You /
->And, faithful God, fetch the dead from the tomb!<-
In dark graves one can indeed never praise You /
->Nor reveal Your wonders to the dead:<-

## The Heavenly Solstice.
<note>original: "Sonnen-Wende." While it means "solstice," it literally translates to "sun-turn," implying the soul turning its face toward God.</note>

O Sun, to whom no brilliance, no light can be compared /
Which always fills pure senses with bright clarity /
Before which whatever darkness and obscurity envelops /
Must vanish and give way like a shadow-image!
Let all the world’s false appearance fade within me /
And command the blinding film to leave my eyes / <note>original: "Blende-Fell," literally a "blinding skin" or "cataract," symbolizing spiritual blindness.</note>
That I may see Your clarity in Your light /
And reach my goal and purpose with a joyful spirit!
Let me, after thunder and lightning, enjoy the gentle sunshine /
After endured agony, enjoy the desired rest!
Then my inner man, like fat olive branches /
Will bloom with eternal green splendor in Your garden:
Let me draw the sap of growth from Your roots /
Then I shall always, my God! show proven fruits.

## XII.

When a light reveals itself in the dark world /

->The Inverted World.<- <note>original: "Die verkehrte Welt." A common Baroque literary theme (mundus inversus) suggesting that earthly life is a topsy-turvy, deceptive reflection of true, divine reality.</note>

The world compares itself nicely to a dark chamber /
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In which what one sees is presented upside down.
For what she calls joy is nothing but bitter misery /
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;What she has raised up is fallen to the ground.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And yet we are blind and believe such trifles <term>trifles: "Tand" refers to worthless trinkets, baubles, or vanity.</term>.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;How here a stream of water wants to run uphill. <note>The image of a river flowing "uphill" was a standard visual shorthand in the 17th century for the "world turned upside down."</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Have pressed into its mind and excellently arranged.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;When one day the eternal day will make all clear.
Just as the light of the sun must illuminate <note>original: "erklären." In this period, the word meant both to explain and to physically brighten or clarify a dark space.</note> the chamber /
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;When one wants to see that which before was entirely dark.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;My poor heart calls to you for faithful assistance:

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;So that I may successfully escape its net!
I see here and there the manifest <note>original: "hellen." While usually meaning "bright," in this context it refers to a crowd that is clearly visible or large in number.</note> crowd of enemies /
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Who have fixed their eyes on me, a poor flea. <note>The "flea" metaphor is a gesture of extreme humility, portraying the speaker as small and vulnerable before both his persecutors and God.</note>

Should I build myself a fortress on light sand?
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;No! it does not endure in the storm and severe weather.

## The Diverse Sowing and Planting.

Pull out, my faithful God, from the garden of my heart
The weeds that the enemy has deceitfully sown,
Which in a very short time sprout up in heaps,
Even when no one diligently tends to them.
So it is! The nettle bush and other wild species
Rise up more and sooner than a good seed,
Which one has planted with great toil and diligence.
God! Let the field of my heart harden like a stone
When Satan stretches his seed over my fallow ground,
And defiles and stains me with hellish poison:
On the other hand, let the seed rise up in full strength,
Which your almighty word scatters into my conscience!
Thus, what delights you and me with sweet pleasure
Will stand like a golden ornament in eternal bloom!

### XIV.

Look at the glass of the earth however you will,
Yet nothing but vanity peers out of every piece,
And a Vesuvius <note>A reference to Mount Vesuvius, the volcano, symbolizing sudden and destructive eruptions of "evil poison."</note> that exhales evil poison,
Which can kill from afar the one who feels secure.

## The Mirror of the World.

->1 John 2:16<- <note>This verse reads: "For everything in the world—the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life—comes not from the Father but from the world."</note>

If one breaks a mirror-glass into many pieces,
And smashes it with a strong hand into small ruins,
One can see his face in every piece,
Along with whatever one happens to be wearing on body and hands.
The world is also like such a mirror,
Which, if the appearance is trusted, lets itself be seen splendidly.
But when one removes the bars of delusion with understanding,
Then it is a false deception, a trifle <note>original: "Tand" — refers to worthless trinkets, toys, or vanity.</note>, not firmly grounded.
Shatter it in your mind, and from all the pieces
(A vain nothingness, which she smears with evil makeup <note>original: "Schmincke" — refers to cosmetic paint used to hide blemishes or create a false face; a common Baroque metaphor for hypocrisy.</note>),
The trifle of vanities and genuine malice will peer through,
And you will see from each what she is plotting <note>original: "was sie im Schilde führt" — literally "what she carries on her shield," an idiom for someone's hidden intentions or schemes.</note>.
We want to devote some time to this labor,
To now examine the body of the great world piece by piece,
And, though unlearned, yet spiritually, to speak of it,
And only briefly pass over a few things.

<header>Appendix of Poetic Poems.</header>

Power, honor, fleshly lust, and an unrestrained life,
The vain service to Mammon <note>A biblical term referring to wealth or property, often personified as a false god that distracts from spiritual devotion.</note> and lewd carnal passion,
These are the things that primarily give the dark world its body.
Look around: what is the world? A great, empty vapor.
O you vain ones, who serve the world so diligently,
And are so devoted to it with your mind and soul!
Look, how a water-stream melts away in swift haste!
Is there anything that can solidify the glass of the world? <note>This refers back to the mirror metaphor on the previous page; "glass" symbolizes the fragile and brittle nature of worldly existence.</note>
Can a king's power exceed the strict law of time—
Which respects neither master, nor servant, nor distinction—
Or the summons of death, with honors?
Why is it then, that man toils after high power?
When pale death now strikes with his scythe,
The master is to him as the servant, the prince as the subject.
Yet one sees how the prince builds himself great palaces,
And boasts of his power, which can help him not at all.
Should base fleshly lust and temporal delight
Be anything better than a piece of vanities?
And should intemperance <term>Unmäßigkeit: lack of moderation, particularly in eating, drinking, or lifestyle</term>, which allows no law to be set for itself,
Should the vain service of Mammon free you from evil?
Should lewd carnal passion prove something precious to you?
O man, the deception of the world is clearer than the sun!
Just let each piece explain itself to you now,
Whether it is not filled through and through with vanity.
The world's power resembles Satan's high ascent,
Which cast him away from God and brought him out of heaven.
What can bend our heart more away from humility
Than a blinded mind that only strives for high status?
Is fleshly lust not an expression of hellish powers?
Whoever loves such pleasure builds himself an eternal grave.
Whoever wishes to fix his goal and purpose in intemperance
Is stupider than a beast and breaks his own neck.
Whoever honors greedy Mammon with a perverted mind,
And sits by his treasure-chests day and night,
He is wounded unto death with hellish poison
And resembles one who sweats in fiery flames.
Teach me, my God, to recognize the world more and more,
And show me the deception in its vanity!
So that my feeble <note>The original German "blödes" in this era meant "weak," "frail," or "simple" rather than its modern meaning of "stupid."</note> heart might not burn itself on her;
Make me ready for your praise and holy service!

When I despise the world and seek to love Jesus,

## Walking with Christ.

My Savior, who has been God from eternity,
And has reigned as King in the great Kingdom,
But who entered into servitude <term>Knechtschafft: the state of being a servant or slave, referring here to Christ's humility on earth</term> during Your time,
So that diseased humanity might recover through You alone;
You never sought Your pleasure in earthly vessels <note>A metaphor for material bodies or worldly possessions.</note>
But always despised the vain world,
And laughed at what brings satisfaction in these times,
Choosing instead only flight, lack, mockery, and the bitter cross:
Let me not commit this error through lack of understanding,
Nor look around longingly for earthly things!
So that I am not caught unexpectedly by deception,
And also become a participant in this carnival play <note>original: "Faßnachtspiel," referring to the rowdy, masked theatrical performances held before Lent, here used as a metaphor for the foolishness and illusions of worldly life.</note>;
Make my mind and spirit free from vain things,
And let me shine here on the cross with heavenly joy!

### XV.

How poor is the fare with which the world pays
The one who, seduced by cunning, gives himself to its service,
And loves its false appearance with hot passion:
Therefore, do not trust it when it boasts with great words!

## The Glory of the World.

Is this now the profit? Are these the great things
With which the false world made you gape your mouth wide?
Did it want to make you free with chains?
Did it honor you with its best fare— { a bitter herb, a piece of tobacco } <note>In the 17th century, tobacco was frequently used in literature as a symbol of "vanitas"—something that turns into smoke and vanishes into nothing.</note>?
O people, learn to recognize the cunning of the world!
When it promises you a sea full of gold and silver,
It intended to include a little piece of steel <note>referring to iron bars or shackles</note> underneath,
Which shatters your structure of freedom with severity.
Like the Sirens <note>Mythological creatures whose beautiful singing lured sailors to their deaths.</note> (who conquer with loveliness),
Covering with waves the one who does not quickly escape:

So the world also wants to sing you a sweet song /
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And strives to capture you through flattery.
She can boast with nectar-juice and honeyed words:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But if you trust her / then a noose is hung around your neck.
For her speech is like poles smeared with lime /
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Where one catches unsuspecting birds with birdlime <note>original: "Vogelleim," a sticky substance used by hunters to trap small birds; a common Baroque metaphor for the traps of sin.</note>:

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;She babbles of heavenly delight and amber-sweet food:
And yet she has crumbled in sorrel and wormwood <note>Bitter herbs representing grief and regret.</note>:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;What she calls nectar is actually just stale, spoiled must.
If she wishes to treat you royally on a holiday /
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Then the first course is merely like tobacco:

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;This is the whole feast / the whole kingdom of pleasure.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;World? shall your grand word be a brazen lie?

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Is that the throne of freedom? Then let the thunder strike it!
Shall bitter tobacco and shackles delight me?
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Shall the smoke constrict my narrow throat?
Do you want to deceive me with acrid vapor and smoke?
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Do you want only to scald me with torment and dungeon-fire?
So cries the poor soul / who, deceived by the world /
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Sits in hell-deep pain and hot misery!
Therefore, whoever trusts her securely has sucked dragon's milk /
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And sprayed his body and soul with eternal poison.
Just as a snare-trigger <note>original: "sprenckel-holz," a wooden part of a bird trap.</note> hinders the bird's freedom /
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;So that henceforth it sees no way for its flight:
So a sea of dungeons has also overwhelmed this man /
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Who does not quickly pull his foot from the world's snare.
With God there is sweet rest and nothing but firm foundations /
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;His eternally holy Word can be nothing but "Amen" <note>Meaning "it is certain" or "so be it."</note>:

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;This only heals the bite of the old serpent <note>A reference to the devil and the fall of humanity in the Garden of Eden.</note>.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Enjoys the delight of eternity even within this time.

A holy heart is often exercised in such ardor <note>original: "Brunst"; in Baroque spirituality, this refers to a fervent, burning love for God rather than carnal desire.</note> /

# Appendix of Poetic Poems.

He who is burdened with a heart of pride's blinding-stone <note>original: "Hoffarts-Blenstein"; likely a metaphorical reference to a heavy, deceptive gem or a weight that blinds the wearer to spiritual truth.</note> /
Is only dragged downward by the heavy weight /
And must bathe his senses in earthly puddles /
The gate and path to heaven’s heights are barred to him.

Even when the Prince of Heaven shows himself in his light /
His proud mind is nevertheless directed only toward the world /
And dances full of joy / as the world plays the fiddle for him <note>original: "vorgeiget"; a metaphor for being led or manipulated by the world's enticing music.</note> /
And follows what she has cunningly devised through false deception.

That is why the world can ensnare with such power /
That whoever trusts her even halfway is immediately bewitched:
He who does not escape her tricks with a high spirit /
Will soon have her witch's poison devastate his entire heart.

He who mirrors himself in her appearance with sweet pleasure /
Has looked into a dazzling-glass <note>original: "Blende-Glaß"; a deceptive or distorting mirror that shows a false image.</note> / that deceitfully lies /
And has unbolted the doors to his own downfall /
And must now go to the grave along with his own salvation.

Man! Do you think that what the mirror-glass presents to you /
Is a true essence in real and right earnest?
Oh no! Deception has joined itself to the delusion /
What you take for truth is but blind masquerade <note>original: "Mummerey"; a carnival-like masking or deceptive play.</note>.

You should not puff up the maggot-sack <note>original: "Madensack"; a common Baroque term for the mortal human body, emphasizing its inevitable decay and lowliness.</note> for much longer /
Even if the false world likens you to an Atlas <note>In Greek mythology, Atlas was the Titan condemned to hold up the celestial heavens.</note>.
He who climbs into the clouds on flat earthly scaffolds /
Has reached only the Tower of Babel instead of Zion's peak.

The sheer vapor of pride cannot make you angelic:
A small dwarf cannot be a giant /
Even if the mirror rouses a proud laugh in him:
It does not make him tall just because he imagines himself to be so.

If you wish to stand by the side of the King himself /
In the wide realm of the holy Cherubim /
Then you must first serve here in deep humility /
And modestly look to the place at the very bottom.

The kingdom of eternity suffers no proud spirits:
What threw Lucifer down from his throne?
Did not the Savior himself and the Master of all lords /
Go with the highest lowliness into a despised grave?

And you, presumptuous one, wish only to parade in pride?
Your proud, cursed heart almost does not know itself!
And yet you still want to receive the beautiful crown there /
Which God has prepared for the lowly through suffering!

### Appendix of Poetic Poems.

But you err / and are dangerously and greatly deceived!
The proud man has no part in God for eternity.
He who has not pulled the yoke of the cross here in humility /
For him, no scepter is prepared in the Kingdom of Joy.
The high God casts the proud from their thrones:
He who honors Him in humility / is made high and great.
Nebuchadnezzar <note>The Babylonian king who was humbled by God and forced to live like a beast (Daniel 4).</note> must dwell among wild beasts;
A poor Joseph is esteemed as equal to the King.
Proud Haman must, on a gallows-oak
(Because he desired to be like God out of arrogance)
Turn pale quite unexpectedly by a hangman’s hand /
And Mordecai <note>The Jewish hero of the Book of Esther who was honored by the Persian king while his enemy Haman was executed.</note> is honored as a Prince of the land.
This, as the final splendor, is pride’s funeral cypress <note>The cypress tree is a traditional symbol of mourning and death.</note>:
He who raises himself too high / falls only that much deeper.
But he who sat here despised in the dust of humility /
For him, a high seat is prepared in that world.

### The Soul Prays for Sanctification.

Oh God! Lock for me the doors of my senses /
So that no false appearance of a perverted world befools me /
Nor Satan’s hellish power harms me with lying-poison /
Nor confuses and misleads me in any other way!
Let my conscience always bear Your faithful witness /
So that at no time I turn out of my bounds /
Nor perhaps be overconfident / and deviate from Your teaching /
Lest, full of trembling, I must feel Your scolding!
Let Your law always be my light and guiding star /
And lead me thereby into the safe harbor!
Let no Lucifer <note>Used here both as the name of the fallen angel and a personification of pride (the "light-bringer" who fell).</note> nest in my heart /
And no vapor of vanity puff me up haughtily /
Let no wind of imagination blow me over /
Nor / whatever else is called sin / devastate my poor heart!

### XVII.

The Italian spider <note>original: "welsche Spinn"; a reference to the Tarantula.</note> sends the one her poison wounds /
Into the dark valley of death / while he laughs joyfully:
So will he / who makes a paradise for himself out of the world /
Also be placed in the deep pit of eternal torment.

## The Great Worldly Deception.

He who once was burned, fears the fire’s smarting;
He who once suffers loss, does not easily go back to it.
He who himself has felt death’s bitter stinging
Takes pity also on those who are troubled:
He who once upon the sea experienced 
The raging of grim waves, and paid his goods as toll to Neptune <note>The Roman god of the sea; here representing the perils of maritime trade and the loss of earthly cargo.</note>,
Cannot base the ground of his hope upon ships,
Nor borrow with profit upon Indian gold <note>original: "Indianisch Gold"; a reference to the riches of the "Indies" (the Americas), which were seen as the pinnacle of worldly wealth and high-stakes colonial enterprise.</note>:
And those who slide upon smooth ice with misfortune,
Choose with wisdom the known path for themselves.
He who cannot step across a wide pit with cunning,
Would rather walk, full of trembling, the narrow and small footbridge.
And if the poisonous world has deceptively lied to you,
You should rightly stay away from it henceforth:
If it has dangerously betrayed you through false cunning,
You should look upon its appearance with Argus-eyes <note>In Greek mythology, Argus Panoptes was a giant with a hundred eyes; the term refers to being hyper-vigilant and seeing through disguises.</note>.
Yet we simpletons trust ice and glass,
And love what merely shines and glitters through deceit.
A wrong path is worth more to us than a secure street:
He who only cheats us bravely, we think has meant it splendidly well.
Are you then blind, O humans? Are you not able to see?
Has the misfortune of others not yet made you wise?
Do you then want to go to ruin just like the others?
Wake up, rouse yourselves: the thunder of collapse is crashing!
The world lies and deceives with nothing but false appearance;
Its life is a death, its sugar a swift poison,
And its lusts are only heavy tombstones;
To whom it gives pleasure, for him it has established his grave-marker.
Learn, humans! Learn to know the world and its varnish <note>original: "Förniß" (modern: Firnis); a metaphor for a deceptive outer coating or veneer that hides a rotten interior.</note>!
There is not a quintel <note>original: "Quintel"; an old German unit of weight (about 4 grams). The poet means there is not even a tiny amount of substance or truth to be found.</note> of substance in its whole being.
Let its false appearance not sever you from God:
Let its deceit be only deceit, and lies be lies!
Shall blinded lust, shall fictional laughter,
And whatever else its mirror-glass presents as joy,
Make you—as you wish—satisfied and truly content?
He who laughs with it, shall be felled along with it.
How! Can the Tarantula <note>Referring to the "Tarantula" spider; in the 17th century, it was believed that its bite caused "tarantism," a state of involuntary, frenzied dancing and hysterical laughter that eventually led to death.</note> stir sweet desire in you?
Shall its desperate poison bid you to be merry?

And does her gall-filled bite move you to dance?
    Her unnoticed sting lays you in the grave.
Thus the poison of the world is accustomed to fatally ensnare us!
    Whoever seeks desired pleasure and sweet joy here,
Wer trusts her brilliance and her cunning tricks,
    Has, out of lack of understanding, cursed what truly gladdens him.
World, boast as you will, you still cannot delight!
    Whoever trusts your words goes merrily to their death.
Those who set the foundation of their desire upon your abyss <note>original: "Ungrund"; literally an "un-foundation" or bottomless pit. It suggests that the world lacks the solid "ground" found in God.</note>,
    Choose, full of joy, bitter mockery instead of well-being.
You have already buried many thousands in the cool sand,
    Who made you into a paradise of proven pleasure:
Until your lying mouth fooled them into the net,
    And killed them eternally in the midst of their pleasure.
Therefore, world, farewell! You shall not delude me,
    Your deception and false dazzle do not harm me.
Your sweet poison and lure-bait <note>original: "Lock-Aas"; a hunting term referring to bait or carrion used to entice an animal into a trap.</note> shall not wound me,
    My heart, mind, and soul stand firmly directed toward God.
Give me, faithful God, to recognize the world rightly,
    And that which flaunts false light through blinding poison:
Let me not be separated from You by what is worldly;
    Then my wish and prayer have reached their goal and purpose!

## The Soul Seeks Protection from the World.

God, You who have set Your throne in Heaven,
    And look down upon the lowly from Your seat,
    You who draw the sorrowful out of their tribulation,
And set free those whom Hell has wounded with its poison!
You see how the world prattles a sweet song to me,
    Though its inner depth drips with bitter gall,
    Which strangles the soul of one who immerses himself in it,
And hunts them into the deep grave of eternal death!
    Be to me a bronze shield and a proven sword,
    That defends me when the world harms me!
Let not its sweet sound lull me into a secure sleep!
    Reveal to me the net that the world has knit for me,
    And has diligently decorated for my downfall:
So I shall not succumb, even when my enemy rages.

### XVIII.

->He who considers himself with much splendor of vanity,<-
->And aims for high things in the heat of pride,<-
->Has recklessly gambled away his noble status,<-

## The Confusion of Babel with its God Mauzzim.

### Genesis 11 <note>original: "1. B. Mos. XI"; referring to the First Book of Moses, Chapter 11.</note>

Up, brother, up! Let us prepare the tough mortar;
->Let everyone be mindful of good bricks!<-
Let us proceed to the magnificent work of the high tower;
->Here a monument of praise shall be established for us forever!<-
Whoever lives after us shall praise our name:
->The peaks of a tower that reaches to the stars<-
Shall show to a distant posterity with wonder
->That this work of ours is like no other!<-
So spoke Babel then, when their proud hearts
->Were dangerously inflated by an empty vapor of pride.<-
Yet, just as a strong wind extinguishes the torch-candles,
->So this deed was also very quickly swept away.<-
The lightning-bolt of the Lord's zeal <note>The "Lord's zeal" refers to divine judgment or righteous anger.</note> descended quickly,
->And made them confused and divided against themselves:<-
A grim sword of confusion cut through the organs of the tongue <note>A poetic description of the "confusion of tongues" where God changed their languages so they could no longer understand one another.</note>
->And Babel was immediately scattered into all the world.<-
Thus is he rewarded, who builds on the tower of Babel!

Make my whole heart pure from all sins;
Let me stand in your house like a pillar /
Which no storm of temptation can twist from its foundation /
Nor a wind of seduction shatter and split apart!
When you set fire to Babel in your wrath /
Then the rock of their hope will vanish like smoke.
Therefore, may you draw my mind to your truth /
And teach me eternal wisdom through your Spirit /
So that I learn to turn away from the world's false appearance /
And flee from all deception at the proper time!

### XIX.

One cannot immediately call what glitters yellow "gold":
For through the cunning of colors, a deception is often made:
Thus the appearance of the world is also falsely held in high esteem /
Even when its things glisten like beautiful gold.

## False Appearance of Godliness <note>original: "Gottseligkeit"; refers to a state of piety or being blessed through devotion to God.</note>, along with its Reward.

Not everything that plays here with beautiful colors /
And creates a magnificent glitter through borrowed appearance /
Has immediately, in deed, achieved the power of gold /
And brought its sought-after praise to the test of affirmation.
Empty shadows often resemble mountains /
Which a pygmy child, full of haughtiness <note>original: "Hoffart"; an archaic term for arrogance or vanity.</note>, casts from himself:
And artificial hair often covers the smooth bald head <note>original: "Platten"; literally "plates," referring here to a bald pate or perhaps a clerical tonsure.</note>:
Many a person has often swallowed poison thinking it was honey.
There is only one single right and true essence <note>original: "Wesen"; the core reality or being of a thing as opposed to its outward show.</note>:
What is not from this is empty vapor and wind.
Whoever wants to gather favorite figs from the hedges <note>A biblical allusion to Matthew 7:16: "Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?"</note> /
Is like-minded to one who is deranged in the head.
What resembles bright light in this gloomy world /
Is but a mockery <note>original: "Affen-spiel"; literally "monkey-play," meaning a foolish imitation or farce.</note> and a shadow-filled night.
The moon has never yet reached the light of the sun /
Nor produced a bright radiance during the day.
When that which stands upon Heaven's foundation and God's Word /
The world stands in its splendor and pure essence:
The spirit of delusion <term>original: "Blendungs-Geist"; a deceptive force that blinds the spiritual or rational "eye" of a person.</term> has immediately twisted an image for her /
Which she strives to honor in place of essence itself.

### XXVI.

Whoever has thrust his neck into the yoke of the world,
Afflicts his soul and disturbs its rest:

-> Worldly Slavery. <-

He whom destiny has sold into slavery,
And led into the valley of misery in shackles;
He sees, sighing, how the stream of his freedom runs dry,
And a weight of chains adorns his neck, hands, and feet.
Whoever is captured by the wild tribe of barbarians,

He cannot so easily regain that peace again,
Which previously made him a master in security.
Just so, he who has once surrendered himself to the service of the world,
And hung its sugared yoke upon his neck,
Can only live in quiet freedom with very heavy effort;
He is sunken into the deep sea of servitude.
It remains true, then, what Paul taught there:
One is called the servant of the one whose will they follow. <note>original: "Man heist desselben Knecht/ dem man zu Willen lebt." Has stuck himself to a burr of servitude.
Therefore, people, you who pledge yourselves to the earth’s yoke,
And yet seek contented rest for your soul!
You have prepared a bitter porridge <note>original: "Muß"; literally a thick pulp or mash, used here metaphorically for a difficult lot or fate one must endure.</note> for yourselves,
And cursed a heavy cross onto your tender neck.
One cannot find sweet honey in a wormwood stalk:
Nor can there be a refreshing julap <term>julap: a sweet, medicinal syrup, often flavored with rosewater, used to soothe or cool the body.</term> in a vinegar jug.

A hard cross presses upon the vainly worldly-minded,
  Even when one sees their body rejoicing in lust.
The imprisoned spirit groans beneath its chains,
  And, oppressed, cries out for rest with a hoarse voice.
Yet nothing at all can rescue it from this distress;
  The malice-filled world stops up both ears.
For she <note>In German, the world (*die Welt*) is a feminine noun and is frequently personified as a deceptive or flighty woman in Baroque poetry.</note> can least of all satisfy our soul,
  Even when man imagines great things from her:
Her entire aim is but shameless deception,
  And she is filled with pure poison and falsehood.
Therefore, whoever gives her loyalty and faith out of a flighty mind,
  Has fashioned a yoke of the cross with his own hand,
And has unhappily fallen in love with Delilah,
  Who, with cursed cunning, brought about Samson’s end. <note>A biblical reference to Judges 16, where Delilah betrays the strongman Samson; here used as an allegory for how worldly desires rob a person of their spiritual strength.</note>
Man, do as you will; if you are possessed by the world,
  Then by force you must be a poor slave,
And forget the joy of your freedom in heart-sorrow,
  Which increases your torment with double pain.
Even if you are blessed with riches for a short time,
  And even if great honors are shown to you in humility:
Yet a heavy cross is entangled therein,
  Which neither high power nor gold can escape.
The turtle must always carry its roof about with it;
  The snail cannot easily leave its house:
Just so, a worldly man cannot drive the cross away from him;
  As long as he loves this world, he must stand at the cross.
Even if a fool wishes to flee from his shadow,
  That which he flees only follows him all the faster.
So too will he strive in vain,
  Who still clings to the world, yet flees from adversity.
The world is nothing but a cross filled with displeasure,
  In her garden grows only eternal hardship.
Therefore, O man, if you desire that which stills your misery,
  Then depart from the world, and follow JESUS!

### The Noble Cross.

My Jesus! only your cross is a sweetened yoke
  And a gentle burden that refreshes my soul,
When the lead of the world presses it into the deep abyss,
  And its weight sinks me into the pit of hell.

## The world is crucified to me, and I to the world.

## The Pleasure of Sin brings forth Death.

AS long as man delights in base pleasure /
And refreshes himself in the paradise of vanity /
He remains entangled in the death-snare of the Evil One /
And has placed himself in the grave of hell.

O woe / to him who thus wounds his heart and mind /
And brings himself out of the quiet sleep of sweet rest!
Whoever entangles himself in this net through recklessness /
Has diligently sharpened the slaughter-sword for himself.

O woe is me / who also lived in cursed pleasure /
And followed after these things, which cloud my conscience!
My **JESUS**, heal me / bind my wounds /
Through the wood <note>Referring to the wooden Cross.</note> that brought you into the grave for us!
Dearest Savior, be mindful now of my salvation!
Here I have / when I am sick / always found medicine.

### XXVIII.

So that the splendor of the earth might force the senses even more /
It puffs itself up with empty wind and light air /
So that they stand truly bloated by the great vapor /
And its deceit-filled death penetrates into secure hearts.

## The World Unmasked.

HOW, World? How? Must you now become your own betrayer?
Has your Argus-cunning <note>A reference to Argus Panoptes from Greek mythology, the hundred-eyed giant. Here it refers to the world's sophisticated and watchful methods of deception.</note> no wakeful eye anymore?
Does the crocodile no longer disguise its gestures? <note>A reference to "crocodile tears," a common metaphor for hypocrisy and deceptive sorrow.</note>
Is your chest of lies then empty of all supply?
Must the empty air now fill you in the sunshine /
So that whatever has eyes can now see your deceit?
Can no curtain hide your false cunning any longer?
What? Or do you now wish to walk in the light of day?
Whereas before, in the dark night of the hard-blinded senses /
(And that was also a piece of your trickery!)
You could begin your sorcery unhindered;
How is it that you now give yourself so boldly and freely?
Quite right! The bright day must drive away your night /
And your peddling <note>original: *Krämerey*. This implies the world is like a merchant selling worthless or deceptive goods.</note> must now go to ruin!
Soon the fair <note>original: *Jahrmarkt*. The "Worldly Fair" was a common Baroque trope representing the vanity and transience of human life.</note> will be entirely canceled for you!
For Light and Will-o'-the-wisp <note>original: *Irrlicht*. A flickering light seen over marshes, used here to represent a false guide or delusion.</note> cannot well stand together.

The Bridegroom <note>A common mystical and biblical image for Jesus Christ, referring to the Parable of the Ten Virgins in Matthew 25.</note> has already put on his clothes /
The radiance / which goes before him / announces his path.
One sees / how you have been so shamelessly deceived until now:
Therefore, let virginity <note>Representing the pure, faithful soul.</note> flee the world / and light the lamp.
She adorns herself for the feast with nothing but white silk /
And wishes to go toward the Bridegroom in her finery.
Therefore, people, up! Do you still want to pasture yourselves in the world?
Do you want to perish with Sodom in the sulfur-fire?
How long then will you trust the false appearance /
Which the eternal day has now brought { into judgment \ to the light }?
Shall the Lord’s axe cut you down with a grim hand /
As He once felled Gomorrah in His wrath?
Oh, do not let your senses be blinded any longer!
Look upon the fraud of the world with wise eyes!
He who / when he sees it coming beforehand / will not turn from the fall;
Has acted even more than equal to a fool.
You see / how the world here boasts of nothing but winds /
With which Fortune has deceitfully filled her:
And whoever performs service for her / is paid only with wind /
With paltry rattling-toys / with which a little child plays.
Ah, so rouse yourself / and let the junk stand!
A Daniel laughs at Babylon’s dragon-game. <note>A reference to the story of "Bel and the Dragon" from the biblical Apocrypha, where the prophet Daniel exposes the trickery of the Babylonian priests.</note>
A Luke cannot depart from his Paul /
Even when Demas over there wants to go to Thessalonica. <note>Referring to 2 Timothy 4:10: "For Demas has forsaken me, having loved this present world... only Luke is with me."</note>
My God! I will lift my lively spirit to you /
I no longer wish to be a citizen here on earth:
My poor heart shall no longer stick to the world;
Let me, unworthy as I am, into your forecourt!
There, one moment shall refresh me many times more /
Than if I were a king here for a thousand years.
Vanity stinks to me / I fear its snares:
Only you / LORD! are my desire: for you I long greatly.
The bloated world of empty vapor and winds
Is to me a bitter cross / a sting / thorn and poison.
O LORD! when will you finally release me from this torment?
When will my ship of hope be brought into the harbor?
Yet let only your will be done! If I must wander here longer /
Then let me always stand in opposition to the world.

Yet when the harvest should come, and one hopes for the fruit of the flames,
The foundation of hope vanishes along with the gain.
What his delighted delusion took for the tincture <term>tincture: in alchemy, a medicinal or metallurgical preparation intended to transmute base metals or heal the body; here used as a metaphor for spiritual perfection</term>,
Is but beautiful shadow-work and does not withstand the test.

And covers his weeping face with a mourning-veil.
But the son of the wise <note>A traditional term for a true alchemist or initiate (Latin: *filius sapientiae*).</note>, who through diligent learning
Reaches the true foundation of things with bitter toil,
Despises the splendor of the shells and chooses only the kernels,
To which white lead and steel show him the certain way.
Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, here symbolizing wisdom or a refined metallic state</note>, whom Mars <note>Representing iron or aggressive force</note> carries away with a strong hand,
He plunges into the deep sea that flows from two salts,
And waits by Vulcan <note>The god of fire, representing the alchemist's furnace or the heat of spiritual purification</note> until she loses her poison,
And finds Mercury’s staff with great joy.
This he binds within a glass, and lets it hang by Vulcan;
Who warms it until everything turns to red dust.
This must then be watered again with its own water:
Thus the artist's toil is honored with more than gold.
This work then withstands the strict tests of the flames,
And is prepared to endure all heat.
Therefore, O Man, if you want God to praise your works there,
Then seek Heaven here, and do not love the Earth!

## The Sharp Fire-Trial.

Let me lead such a life in this time,
That I strive for the noble gold of the highest virtue,
And always live so pure and holy before You, my God,
That there a laurel wreath may adorn my brow!
He who wallows without understanding in the red of sin <note>original: "Sünden-Roth"</note> like irrational beasts,
And roots around in the earth,
Has—to his eternal shame—lost his entire game,
When the strict law of fire shall test him.
Woe to him who resembles light straw and empty stubble,
When the Judgment of Wrath creeps upon him with hot flame!
How shall a sinner stand before his God!
For he who has spent his life in vanity,
Will be made a thing of shame and mockery at that trial,
When one day everything must pass through the fire.

# Appendix of Poetic Poems.

### XXX.

A heart that is radiated by the brilliance of the Godhead,
The soul, which is filled with the delight of heaven,
Can henceforth no longer be enveloped in empty vapor,
Nor painted with the pale color of the shadow-nothingness.

### The Reward of Victory for a Heroic Christian.

Triumph! Triumph! Triumph! Malice is avenged;
The empty glass of the world is (thank God!) fallen:
The shadow-rich nothingness of the earth is broken,
And its deceptive poison brought to the light of day.
Arise, soul, tread upon the enemy with brave, heroic feet!
Who lies languishing before you, and cries out <note>original: "schneidt"; likely a typo or archaic variation of "schreit" (cries/shouts), though it literally translates to "cuts." In this context, it refers to the enemy's final lament or death-cry.</note> his funeral dirge;
The strength of his power is torn apart by the victory,
Which the strong God gives to you in His light.
What Joshua did, when he banished the wild herds
Of the Canaanites <note>The biblical account of Joshua leading the Israelites to conquer the Promised Land.</note> there with fire and sword;
What Gideon did, when he became Israel's commander,
And destroyed and overthrew the army of Midian:
The immense power of the grim, wild Moors <note>original: "Mohren"; a historical term used here to refer to the Cushite (Ethiopian) army led by Zerah.</note>,
Whom Zerah brought to the field against Israel,
And who were dreadfully lost through the army of Asa <note>King Asa of Judah, who defeated a numerically superior force according to 2 Chronicles 14.</note>,
Is rightly considered a triumph and a great victory.
One holds the excellent and wonderful deeds,
Which Maccabeus <note>Judas Maccabeus, the Jewish guerrilla leader who led the revolt against the Seleucid Empire.</note> dared there with good fortune,
And which turned out to the great salvation of the land,
In high renown, because he thereby chased away the power of the enemy.
Yet all this is to be regarded only as a meager thing,
Which does not yet by far equal the true battles:
When we properly consider the hard war of souls,
And their laurel wreath, which they achieve through victory.
He who has overcome the world with a courageous spirit,
And has slain its vain deception with bravery,
Has truly fettered and bound an enemy
Who always carries the coat of arms of Hell in his banner.
O glorious triumph! To overcome the world,
To scatter the strong power of Hell with joy,
To bind the strength of the enemy's army in chains and fetters;
Let no one tell me those are common victories!

# Appendix of Poetic Poems.

Now, just as a king is accustomed to reward heroes
Who have heated themselves with honor in the hard struggle:
So the Lord of Lords also grants noble crowns
To those who, until the enemy was scattered, sweated in sour combat.
A faithful heart, which has torn itself away from the evil world,
Sits in the heavenly fortress upon a throne of victory,
And treads upon the exhausted enemy with bold heroic feet:
Whoever overcomes in this way, receives such a reward.
Thus, whoever has earnestly fought the good fight here,
Shall joyfully put on the prepared crown:
Thus the hardship of the earth is now subdued;
Thus laughs he, who here often moistened himself with hot tears!
Therefore, people, if you wish to be called famous heroes there,
If you wish to be adorned there with laurels and crowns;
Then you must truly clash with your enemy here,
And endure a blow that leads to honor.
Here you must magnanimously overcome Hell and the world,
And always in hot combat { walk upon pale corpses, }

And struck down the power of all enemies with great praise:
Let me, as long as I must still struggle in this time,
Be neither faint, nor full of fear, nor weary, nor tired!
May You, as Moses did there, spread out Your hands for me, <note>A reference to Exodus 17, where Moses held up his hands to ensure the victory of the Israelites over the Amalekites; as long as his hands were raised, they prevailed.</note>
So shall I enter as a victor with triumph!

# Appendix of Poetic Poems.

Do you seek pleasant delight in sugar-sweet joys,
When He, the Savior, is despised with scorn and mockery?
Do you wish to walk with a proud gait upon beautiful flowers,
When He carries the hard Cross toward Golgotha?
Should a throng of servants stand bowed before you,
When His bloody head is struck with iron fists?
Do you wish to dance in the lust of the flesh with crooked leaps,
And rejoice in excess and gluttony,
When sharp lances pierce His pale body,
And His dry tongue must be parched and thirsty?
Do you wish to adorn your proud corpse in the pomp of vanity,
And stand in silk and purple with a painted head,
While spittle-filth smears His face?
Should He be stripped, and perish naked and bare?
No, this does not rhyme! <note>original: "reimt sich nicht" — a play on words; while it means the logic "doesn't add up," it also refers to the poetic structure of the text itself.</note> That which touches the Lord
Rightly befalls the servant who loves his Master.
If the Master has been led through the bitter Cross,
Then the disciple also may not remain untroubled.
The Cross can indeed drive away the tickle <note>original: "Kützel" — a physical sensation of itching or tingling, used here metaphorically for the tempting urge of worldly desire.</note>
Which evil lust awakens in our flesh:
Through the Cross we can numb the wild body,
And tame the desire that dwells in the limbs.
Therefore, **Jesus**! Through Your Cross, which pressed upon Your neck,
Crush that which wishes to pull me toward the lust of the flesh!
Through Your crown of thorns, which pinched Your head,
Sustain me when I wish to flee from the Cross!
The lance with which Your side was pierced,
Stab through that which in me is inclined toward pride!
Through Your martyrdom, which broke Your heart,
Crush what shows a worldly life in me!
Thus shall what is earthly be turned away from my soul, <note>original: "gedrechselt" — Continuing the "lathe" metaphor from the previous page, suggesting the soul is a piece of wood being reshaped by a craftsman.</note>
The shavings of this world profitably cast off,
And renewed and changed into another image,
That remains eternally, and can never be corrupted.

## Recognizant Gratitude of the Soul for her Conversion.

Now world, farewell! I depart with heart and mind
From your deceit’s perverted Babylon; <note>Babylon is used here as a traditional biblical metaphor for a place of sin, confusion, and exile from God.</note>

Wounded to the core from the quiver of His passion: <note>original: "Brunst" — while often meaning physical heat or lust, in this mystical context it refers to the burning, intense fire of divine love.</note>

And was among grim wolves without shepherd or protection,

As if a wild steed, I tore the reins asunder,
And like a lustful stallion followed my own desires:
When I was busily devoted only to evil,
And already began to sink into the abyss of hell:
Your burning heart called me back,
And placed a new bridle in my mouth!
You have raised me from the grave onto heaven’s high steps,
And put to death that which torments my soul!
Should I now—who am filled with heaven's costly, precious treasures
And drunk from the wine
Of sweet eternity—still set my heart
Upon the world's cold ice and be devoted to it?
Ah, no! Whoever has once tasted the liquid honey,
Which already gives us a foretaste of angelic joy,
Will no longer be stained by the world's gall-poison,
Nor saddened by the wormwood-drink of vain pleasure.
Whomever the Shulamite’s friend <note>A reference to the Bridegroom in the Song of Solomon, interpreted in Christian mysticism as Christ.</note> leads into his cellar,
And makes drunk from the sweetness of the wine,
Will no longer be led astray by the world’s bitterness,
Nor brought out of his rest by vain trifles.
World, do you dare to storm my heart?
You fish in the air and labor in vain.
Whomever Salem’s <note>original: "Salem" — an ancient name for Jerusalem, here signifying the heavenly city of peace.</note> thousand shields and sharp swords protect,
Is safe, even when he sees the storm approaching.
If before this you could easily deceive me,
Your deception has now reached its end.
Henceforth you must lie bowed beneath me,
And see how your luster pales before my Sun.
A steel more than firm has guarded my breast,
The bright helmet of salvation has covered my head:
The strong shield of love, which pairs itself with faith,
Has awakened all that I am and can do to bravery.
Therefore, I now bid you defiance! <note>original: "Troß" (modern: Trotz) — a cry of challenge or defiant provocation.</note> Defiance, that your murderous tumult
And your army’s power enter the battle with me!
Defiance, that the Devil’s power with his nightly swarm
Should dare to fell me with deceptive appearance!
Because JESUS has taken possession of my mind, sense, and heart,
I am freed from the world and its wrath,
And have come to the silent rest of the angelic host,
Where one cries Hallelujah with a joyful throat!
